speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: PROVISION OF MARRIED QUARTERS FOR PERSONNEL OF ARMED SERVICES AND DEFENCE RESEARCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of its important relationship to the whole question of housing, I would like to announce to the house a very large addition to the program of construction of married quarters for personnel of the armed services and defence research. This will call for completion this year of 2,350 new houses in thirty-six different localities, at a cost of approximately $20 million. This will be a direct contribution to relief of housing shortages in civilian communities, as the moving into service married quarters will make housing available for civilian families.
On January 1, 1947, the armed forces had 1,241 married quarters. By March 31, 1948, 2,863 units were added and 1,864 were under construction, of which 1,179 were new houses, making, with the 1,171 to be begun after April 1, 1948, a total of 7,139 married quarters. These new houses are allocated on the basis of need, not rank, and rental rates will be the normal quarters allowance.
I am making available to hon. members a statement giving particulars of this program, which is one of the largest housing projects undertaken in Canada, and is part of the effort to provide as far as possible the condition of normal family and community life for armed forces personnel, particularly in remote areas.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Last evening, Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned, I was discussing the budget; I mention that just in case someone may have forgotten. I had concluded my remarks on the Conservative amendment and was suggesting seriously to them that they might withdraw that amendment and get it out of the way, so that we might take all the discussion on the subamendment proposed by the members of this group. I suggested that because we definitely recommend something that the government did not include in the budget. Second, I was pointing out some of

The Budget-Mr. Gillis
the disabilities of the budget, as I see it. In concluding my remarks of last night I took a few minutes to point out that a table put on Hansard by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), when he made his budget speech, suggested that the tax rates in the United States were much lower than they were in Canada. I also put a table on Hansard having to do with the category of a married person with two children. It showed quite definitely that the tax rates in Canada in that group are much higher than they are in the United States.
I personally feel that the government made a mistake in not giving some relief to those in the low-income tax brackets. I say that for this reason. During the year 1947 the real wages of those in the low-income tax brackets were cut drastically by the increase in prices. We hear a good deal in this house about initiative and incentive. I think that the graduated form of tax as applied to the industrial workers, the farmers and fishermen, who in the final analysis produce all the real wealth of the country, militates against initiative and incentive. I know that many times during the war we seriously suggested to the government that it would be much better to impose a flat rate and make a cut-off at some point, where overtime work was necessary-that is, when during the war you wanted workers in industry to work a great deal of overtime. The same thing applies now.
For the minister's benefit, so that we may be able to amend the section dealing with exemptions, I should like to say this-and I am going to deal now with the part of the country from which I come. I have here an analysis made by the research director of the mine workers, taken from government statistics, which points out definitely that real income in Nova Scotia has been reduced drastically by inflationary prices. It reads:
From November, 1946, to December, 1947, average earnings of 75,000' workers in Nova Scotia increased by $2.07 per week, or by 6-7 per cent. During the same period the government cost-of-living index climbed 21-2 points or 17 per cent.
This means that real weekly earnings in Nova Scotia fell during 1947, by as much as 10 per cent.
For the low income family with more than the average number of children the decline in living standards was much more than 10 per cent.
The minister should at least consider keeping living standards where they were in 1947. Unless there be some move on the government's part to increase the exemption in the low-income groups, there must be a drastic reduction in the living standards of the people in that income group.
To continue-and this is from the same
source:
During the year 1947 the cost-of-food index increased by 24 per cent, and clothing by 23 per cent.
I should like to bring sharply to the minister's attention the fact that ninety per cent of the wages of those in the income group under $1,500 or $2,000 a year goes into food and clothing; and those increases of 24 per cent and 23 per cent brought about a considerable reduction in the standard of living in 1948 as compared with 1947. These are commodities that are on the table of the average working person in this country every day. The exemption from excise or sales tax will not affect these items to any great extent, because, as the minister pointed out, while he is relieving some food items from sales tax, the exemption may not be reflected in the price structure. My guess is that it will not. It will be added to it, because no one in this country today can tell anyone else what price he must charge for any given commodity.
I think that the exemption levels that were advocated by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell)- $1,250 for a single person and $2,500 for married persons-would compensate the taxpayer to some extent for the increase in the cost of living and the lowering of living standards in 1948 for that income group, and would also create some incentive and initiative. But if you are to keep dragging them down, without any recognition, then you are just creating frustration and hopelessness in this country.
I cannot understand the attitude or the mentality of the minister's advisers who suggested that the exemption for persons who are sixty-five years of age and older should be increased by $500 a year. That suggestion might have come from gentlemen in the other place. Most of them will be relieved.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suggest that after serious reflection, instead of making that increased exemption applicable to the age group sixty-five and over, which does not mean anything, the minister might see his way clear to extend the $500 exemption to the income groups recommended by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar and step up the exemptions to $1,250 and $2,500. In that way the minister would create incentive. Thousands of young people across this country, men and women, are on low incomes. Many of them would like to get married, make a home, and take their part as citizens of this country. But when they look at the tax structure; when they see the little consideration that is given by persons in high places to the question whether they shall be able to live a full and complete life, they are afraid to take a chance. An increase in the exemptions would encourage people to drive their roots into the soil and really become citizens of the country. There is fear and frustration among many in the low-income groups. To increase the exemption would assist the thousands of families who have suffered a substantial reduction in their standards of living because of the increased prices of the necessities of life which they must provide for themselves and their children. Again, many families would be able to keep their children in school if they had that relief. For humanitarian reasons, therefore, if for none other, I believe the minister should take this suggestion into serious consideration. That is the one quarrel we have with the budget under the present mechanics of society. In my opinion the minister was short-sighted and ill-advised, because I know that in view of increased prices and the lowering of standards which has resulted, the people were looking for some relief through increased exemptions for the low-income groups.

I am not going further with that line of criticism. As I pointed out last evening, the budget itself is merely a statement made by the government to the country, showing what they have done in the field of finance. My quarrel with that sort of budgeting is that in addition to a financial statement from the government I believe it is also a part of the responsibility of the government to the people, in a country such as this, that the Minister of Mines and Resources, or some other minister who may be charged with the responsibility, should bring into this house a capital budget which would take the resources of this country as between province and province and endeavour to develop those resources in order to make for equality in the distribution of income, so far as that can be achieved. Certainly the distribution of income is badly out of line today. We are living in an age when the planning of our resources and their proper development are absolutely essential.
Some members of this house may say: Well, we do not believe in planning. But I noticed yesterday that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) told the house he was bringing in a bill for the purpose of planning the national capital. Surely if the government thinks the planning of this one city as a national capital requires legislation to be passed by this house, setting up a commission and all the rest of it, then the same principle should be followed in the whole economic set-up of this country. If it is essential to plan the capital city of Ottawa, surely it is much more essential that the government, which is charged with the responsibility of exploiting the resources of the country and is the custodian of those resources, should take steps to see that there i3 justice and equality as between the different sections of the country. I suggest that this kind of capital budget should be brought in also.
I say that for the reason that I come from the maritime provinces. I am sorry so few of the members from the maritimes are vocal in regard to the problems and disabilities of that end of the country. Yesterday afternoon the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) fully justified the present budget, as I said last night, based on the maintenance of the status quo. As I think the minister himself asked at one time, "What is the status quo"? That is the mess we are in; but he justified it on the basis that we are going to stay as we are, that we are not going to make any changes. On that basis he made an excellent speech and an excellent case for the budget. But if we are to remedy some of the injustices that exist under the present system, we cannot just stop there.

The Budget

Mr. Gillis
I have in my hand a government publication released a few weeks ago. It comes from the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, and is entitled "The maritime provinces in their relation to the national economy of Canada." The opinions expressed in this publication therefore come from the government. I have gone through it very carefully, and for the benefit of the Minister of Finance I should like to point out some of the economic and social c'onditions that exist in our end of the country. We must remember that the minister, whether he comes from Westmount or from Vancouver, represents all people of this country, including the maritimes, in the finance department. Perhaps the reason he is not paying more attention to the maritimes is that apparently many maritime members are quite satisfied. You know, you do not get a seat in the senate by quarrelling with the government about disabilities that may exist in your part of the country. Here is just an extract from this report; I could pull out dozens of them, but I am going to give just a few which rather stand out, touching various social and economic aspects down there. The first one is at page 29:
The proportion of persons in the younger and older age groups in the maritimes is above the national average, while for the in-between ages the proportion in the maritimes is considerably below the -all-Canada figure. The latter reflects the exodus from the maritimes of workers in the prime of life. They leave after having been educated at the expense of the provinces and when young, vigorous, ambitious, and enterprising. By their departure the maritimes lose not only .the most efficient type of workers, but also the enterprising lability important to further development. Their loss reduces, too, the taxable capacity of the region, a fact which is all the more serious in view of the large proportion which the dependent groups-the children and the aged-constitute of the total population of the region. Persons below' the age of 15 comprise 3-0-2 per cent of the total population in Prince Edward Island, 29-2 per cent in Nova Scotia, and 31-9 per cent in New Brunswick-
As compared with 5-2 per cent in Saskatchewan and Alberta. The point I am trying to make for the benefit of the minister is that the productive people of the maritime provinces are obliged to leave that part of the country. What we have there are the youth, those in school whom we are educating. We are spending our resources on them. When these young people are educated we lose to the United States about 15,000 of them every year. We have been doing that for the last thirty years.

No, it is not because the war is over. There is a greater market in the world today for fish than there was when the war was on. As I have said, production increased by 196 per cent between 1938 and 1945, and since the war it has gone back to about where it was in 1938. These figures indicate, all the way through, the inequality of the distribution of income in different industries. For instance, ten per cent of the population of Nova Scotia are engaged in agriculture, but we receive only 4-6 per cent of the national income from the field. If we were receiving our just due we would have at least ten per cent of the national income. Therefore, I say agriculture is away down. The same ratio would apply in manufacturing, and in all other lines of endeavour.
Let me make it clear to hon. members from Quebec and Ontario that as one of the members from the maritime provinces I am not asking for anything more than a square deal.
I would say this to them, that the base for many of their industries in Quebec and Ontario came from the maritime provinces in the first instance. The production is siphoned off by centralization.
Again, in this statistical report-

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
I will conclude by reading briefly from the statistical report in support of my contention
[Mr Isnor.]
that centralization of industry in Canada, short-sightedness and lack of planning on the part of those in authority, are responsible for the difficulties of the maritime provinces. We find this at page 96 of the report:
Concentration grew through the agglomeration process,-
That is a good word; look it up in the dictionary.
-the tendency of manufacturing and service industries to concentrate where there is already some concentration of industry because of the greater availability of labour, managerial and technical skills, industrial and financial and other services. Moreover, the central provinces are geographically-
Remember this; listen to it.
-an extension of the greatest industrial area of the United States.
The concentration in Ontario and Quebec is considered merely as an extension of the industrial area of the United States.
-a fact which undoubtedly stimulated the industrial development of these provinces. United States capital and the establishment of branch plants contributed to the same result.
I shall not read further from the report. I hope, however, that some of the maritime members will make a check of the survey and examine the disabilities outlined in this economic and social survey of the maritime provinces.
I suggest seriously to the minister that that problem has been further aggravated by the increase in freight rates. The picture today for the maritime provinces is bleak indeed, unless the government is prepared, as I suggested a moment ago, seriously to consider bringing in a capital budget to the house which will give to the maritime provinces greater equality of distribution of income and a greater decentralization of industry which has been concentrated in the central provinces. For example, we should break the integration of the two economies and try to stand Canada on her own feet as a nation.
I could go on for some considerable time with this subject, but I shall not. I thank the house for the short extension of time that has been given me.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do not intend to burden the house, if I can avoid it, with repetition of what has already been said. I had not thought of speaking on the budget until I listened to the rather spectacular speech that was made yesterday afternoon by the Minister of Justice.
The budget has been the subject of great national concern, as it properly should be and has been on many other occasions. It is per-

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
haps the largest budget we have had in normal times, and it is a very interesting document. Some have called it a vinegar budget; some have called it a black budget, and I believe the minister has almost admitted that it is an austerity budget. In looking it over and finding that the consumer's dollar is worth only two-thirds of what it was a few years ago, and that there is very little direct relief, one might term it a Black Douglas budget. However, I do find disguised and almost hidden in it a semblance of the old traditional policy of Liberalism, despite the quotas, restrictions and prohibitions. I notice that some duties have been removed, and it is interesting to know that we can now get beeswax and mulberry trees in free. It is an indication that the old dusty doctrine of free trade is not quite dead.
Despite all that has been said, and the almost reckless disregard some have when dealing with billions or hundreds of millions, one is reminded of Canada's greatness and her ability to withstand such a spectacular experiment. This is indeed a great country. I believe that all this country needs is the magic of confidence in ourselves and in our development. Undoubtedly we have more resources than any other country with a similar number of people. Members of this house have basic and common interests and desires for the development of our resources, the employment of our people, their prosperity and security, and indeed national unity as well; therefore I thinik we are justified in criticizing policies which do not enhance these developments.
We need stability to replace fear and doubt and uncertainty. We need steadiness to replace changes, hectic and reckless as sometimes they appear to be. We hear a great deal about our national pride. We have the minister of external affairs and others talking about our foreign policy and the great part we have to play in world affairs. We sometimes seem to forget that we are just 13,000,000 people. We are reminded of this when we try to match armies overseas with other large powers.
It is a fine thing to have national pride, but it would be a greater thing in this era of change and transition to have a little more national policy and a little less boastfulness about our national pride. I think we should have more national thinking in our economy in Canada and less international dreaming and theorizing as to what we will do in some great world conflict side by side with other nations of 130,000,000 or 140,000,000 people.
Under the regime of those to your right, sir, every year since they have been in power the number of people leaving this country to find 5849-283i
employment has been almost more than those graduating from our universities. It is time we began thinking in Canadian terms and having more of the confidence that is essential to our development to which I have referred, and the stability that is required to meet our great obligations.
Stability cannot be restored by borrowing $300 million from a foreign country to maintain an artificial or dishonest dollar here at home. Trade cannot be developed by putting a twenty-five per cent excise tax on our production at home and then putting quotas and restrictions by ministerial decree on articles coming in. Trade has never been built up in that way. I have listened for many years to the great apostles of free trade who have told us that they will reach out to all the corners of the earth and sell what they can sell for ihe most money and buy what they need for the least money. But I am amazed to find that under ministerial decree we have quotas, restrictions, restraint, and strangulation of trade. Then in order to stop production at home we put on a special excise tax of twenty-five per cent on our requirements; and this at a time when other ministers are talking about the high cost of living. I refer to the tax imposed on frigidaires, vacuum cleaners and kitchen utensils.
Confidence cannot be restored in the development of our great resources, by so few people, by taking $670 million a year more from the people than is required. It is fine to talk about having a surplus, but that is just like a' man going to the bank and borrowing $5,000 more than he needs so that he will think he is richer than he was before he left home. Confidence is not encouraged in that way. It is not encouraged either by a difference of opinion among cabinet ministers. It is not encouraged or sustained by political expediency conflicting with government policy. It is not sustained by the Prime Minister making a speech in Geneva and saying we are going to have great international trade, and the Minister of Finance saying at home that we are to have quotas and prohibitions to stop trade. Those things do not help.
A week before the budget the Prime Minister brought down a great health program. We have had periods of progress in this country toward social reform every time there is a provincial election, every time there is a byelection, every time there is a dominion election. It is then that we make strides toward taking a social interest in our people.
I have listened to the same old story every year from 1919. What about Drew? He will
The Bridget-Mr. Rowe

be the next premier of Ontario, and his opposition will be doing as his other opposition did- listening to the grass grow on his beautiful farm.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what happened to you one time.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The iron, member never got that far. I am not going to be distracted by those who want amusement rather than enlightenment.
The Prime Minister talks of spending millions on health, and yet the Minister of Finance thinks that over and above the expenses of government he must take $670 million from us because we do not know how to spend it. When they are in a hurry they do not need to get provincial approval, but for twenty-nine long years from 1919, action of this kind could not be taken without provincial approval. Now when these old, weary statesmen of the sea begin to see the danger signs in the offing, when they see that there is no chance of retrieving the situation in the province of Ontario, when they see that it is doubtful that they will win any one of the three by-elections, then the Prime Minister says: I promised that in 1919; it was part of my old chart and compass. The ship of state has been drifting around the islands of by-elections in the meantime, but we must pull that one out now.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, they talk about inflation. The ex-minister of finance, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) referred to it yesterday. Hon. members remember how serious he got. He talked about intellectual honesty. I often wish I belonged to some of the fraternities as he does, so that I could get as serious and sanctimonious, and thus make men believe me.

speechtext:
You may win some, but you will not win as many as you think, and you will be lucky yourself if you come back here.
This country needs a government that will keep a strong hand on the helm. We are drifting apart. Our unity is disturbed. Two provinces are out in the cold on the tax agreements. Seven provinces are rudely snubbed on the freight rates issue. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party played ball with the communists until the communists left and tried to play with the C.C.F. Now nobody knows who owns the child. Anything to keep in power.
Let me return now to dominion-provincial affairs, and all these private deals of horse trading-and I know something about horse trading. I know that when you get behind the box-stall door you can make a deal if you give the other fellow enough to boot. It is amusing to realize that when these trades were made behind the box-stall doors in secret conferences-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No secret conferences at all.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not secret-private deals; the public found out afterwards, you mean. In the final deal the dominion collects seven times as much as it pays to British Columbia, five times as much as it pays to Manitoba, I believe about three times as much as it pays to some of the other provinces, and one and a half times as much as it pays to one province. How much am I bid? Going at $1.50; make it $3; make it $7, if necessary. If these provinces had known, they would have made it $9. I would like to be negotiating with you fellows on these deals. I am not at all surprised that our able premier in Ontario cannot negotiate with you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Neither am I.
The Budget-Mr. Rowe

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did not expect you would be. I believe I have a clipping here from one of your splendid papers. It is a good paper, and it is getting better all the time- the Vancouver Sun, which says, "Hello Sucker!" I will not take the time to read the article. After all, about the only thing that is free in the country now is the press.
In my opinion the government has not very much to boast about, so far as dominion-provincial relations are concerned, in respect to the type of deals to which I have referred. The confidence of the people is not strengthened when the Minister of Agriculture says he will bring in from 12,000,000 to 15,000,000 people to eat our wheat in Canada, and the minister of reconstruction, or the minister of many activities, states that the immigration problem should be left to the provinces.
I am bound to say, Mr. Speaker, that I followed with keen interest the speech made yesterday by the Minister of Justice. I was going to refer to this before now, because I had expected he would return. I have always appreciated the intellectual honesty he spoke about, but I was getting rather confused when he talked yesterday about intellectual honesty, when he said that no one on this side of the house had opposed the revaluation of the Canadian dollar. I remember that on the night it was announced-and, by the way, they must have known about it first on the Montreal stock exchange and in Toronto, because stocks reacted seriously that day- when someone on this side of the house wanted to oppose it, he was howled down by the cheer-crier who saved my hon. friend on so many occasions last night.
I do not doubt the honesty, intellectual or otherwise, of the Minister of Justice. He is a grand gentleman. I must say, however, I was amused last night when he said he was not sure whether his judgment or his memory was failing him. As I listened I thought they were both going, because I could not help thinking-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But that was not what he said.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-that he was on a sort of sightseeing tour, the "mystery" tour you sometimes see advertised here. As he went on that mysterious tour he was trying to find excuses for the errors that have been committed by his government, and he went back to July 5, 1946, when he said he did not think that ten per cent either way meant so much. Premier George Drew said it might mean $100 million more, but the right hon. gentleman said he read in a Toronto paper-probably the Tele-

gram or the Star, but an evening paper-an estimate of only $15 million having been suggested, and he said that Premier Drew had no basis in reason for saying that we would have had $100 million more.
On July 5, 1946, when our dollar was revalued at 100 cents, at an artificial value, a dishonest value, it was reported by some that many persons in the department believed that the dollar might go back to sixty-five cents. I think that was absurd, but they were afraid it would go to eighty cents and they thought they would put it at 100 cents and bluff it there. It was mysterious indeed, and it is of great significance, because it was a great change, it was a great risk born of a great fear. It was the putting back of controls when we were told that we were leaving controls. The action was taken because we did not want inflation ; we wanted more production at home and less buying abroad; and so they told the people: We will make your dollar worth more where you want to buy and worth less where you want to sell.
It was a new type of economy, apparently, on the part of a controller whose influence is great around here. Probably he was born since I came here first. As I listened to the Minister of Justice I could not help thinking that in the first half of his speech, his voice sounded like the voice of the minister, whereas, in the latter half the hand seemed to be the hand of the deputy minister of finance.
We all know-these are tragic, historical truths by this time-that in the sixteen months subsequent to July, 1946, no matter what anyone says he thinks will happen, what actually did happen was that $1,100 million of American reserves disappeared. We know that we were that much short, $60,000,000 or $70,000,000 per month. The primary producers across the dominion paid a still greater penalty for this novel type of experiment. We know that it encouraged imports, because imports increased; it discouraged exports, and moreover, it very nearly ruined the great gold mining industry of the dominion.
In the old days, when people wanted to praise something, they said that it was as good as gold, and then it was as good as wheat in the bin. We heard investments talked about last night as speculative. We do not consider United States investments speculative; for the fact is that some $7 billion of United States money has helped to make this country what it is.
I listened to the manifestation of intellectual honesty of the Minister of Justice last night when he told us that taxes were higher in the United States than in Canada. Of course you can add up a set of taxes and

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
show almost any figure, and figures do not lie, even though some people figure. But, Mr. Speaker, the minister did not tell you last night that we have a sales tax in Canada. And, by the way, I remember hearing what the Prime Minister used to say when I first came here. I wish the right hon. gentleman were here now, because, as I well remember, he almost wept over the fact that we had a sales tax of two per cent in 1921 and in 1925. It was terrific. In 1935 we were told that we were ruining the people, we were strangling trade, because there was a five per cent sales tax. Now we have a sales tax of eight per cent, and the Prime Minister does not weep at all.
These political twists, turns and manoeuvres are all interesting and no less expensive to the Canadian people, but last night I was more disturbed than I was interested when I heard the Minister of Justice say that we had to be so careful. So that I shall not misquote him,-because I have some intellectual honesty too-I wish to quote his views: "But it would be undesirable, I feel sure, having in mind public opinion in the United States, to have a situation arise such as this: that the people in the United States should be keeping their taxes up to the high levels they have now attained, and that Canada, not contributing toward European recovery by way of credits, should seize the opportunity to push taxes down and cash in on the situation in such a way that we would inevitably be severely criticized and penalized by others." I have been a long time in this house, Mr. Speaker, but I have never witnessed a spectacle which more conspicuously illustrated an inferiority complex in relation to a foreign power than that. Surely, by that quirk of policy, the Minister of Justice is not going to force me, after all these years of campaigning in Ontario, to go to the western states and campaign among the farmers there to see if they will allow their congressmen to allow Canada to lower tariffs. It is so ridiculous that I am afraid that some scarcely comprehend the significance of it. I feel that we would be laughed at in Washington. If I made that statement in Dufferin-Simcoe, I am sure I would be laughed at; worse than that, I would not get back here. But, Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member does not know what we think.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. I think you think about
the same.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But we don't say anything.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, you don't say anything, but you think a lot. I do not blame you. The
loyalty to leadership is marvellous. You think as you like, but you vote with your leader.
The present Minister of Justice has no monopoly on this at all, because when the twenty-five per cent excise tax was put on the new home builder, the Minister of Finance stated on December 16, 1947, his second reason for these taxes. These are taxes that were put on by order in council, by radio or telephone; I think the Toronto Star had them first, but they were put on anyway, and were collected before they were passed on by parliament. They were to be returned if they were not passed. They finally got through. These were the novel taxes that had to be put on quickly. This is what the Minister of Finance said, as reported at page 336 of Hansard of December 16, 1947:
A second reason for these taxes was to limit so far as practicable the degree of discrimination-
Follow this, Mr. Speaker:
-against regular suppliers in the United States and their dealer organizations in Canada. For the time being, many of these suppliers and dealers are losing a part of their business because of the unavoidable necessity of restricting imports from the United States. Regrettable as it is, we cannot help that. But by imposing these excise taxes we are doing something to protect the legitimate longer-range interests of these businesses.
There we have two ministers who are in unison at least on one thing. You can call it whatever kind of budget you like, but it looks like a made-in-Washington budget. It is not novel with the two ministers today, because prior to 1934 I sat in this house and listened to what the present Prime Minister had to say when the Hawley-Smoot tariff closed our markets in the United States to Canadian farmers. The Prime Minister said that we dare not raise tariffs against the United States at this time for fear we provoke the United States of America. I should like to ask the new aspirant for leadership, the Minister of Agriculture, if he agrees with that.

I will not take long. I do
not want to debate the matter of how much time I have left. Some say seven minutes and some say three. In view of your courtesy, Mr. Speaker, I will conclude as quickly as possible.
I asked the Minister of Agriculture if he agreed. I know the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice agree, and I expect the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) would agree. If they all agree, then I am not much surprised that it was reported the other day in the papers that the present Prime Minister, when he looks over these aspirants to carry the mantle of leadership of the once great Liberal party, is in more distress than ever, and says: "Anyway, no matter who takes it on, I will have to carry on as prime minister." I am not surprised.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is a good one.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That gives you encouragement, because no doubt you cannot miss if you can pass excuses on to him for a while. I notice that the Winnipeg Free Press mentions this matter on May 20, on the editorial page, in the following words:
The position of Mr. King's successor, a man chosen by the party in office to lead it in the House of Commons, would be in a strange position indeed if he were not Prime Minister, and if a statesman no longer a party leader were still head of the government. Under our parliamentary system, power must go with responsibility.
The Winnipeg Free Press believes that. But with the bureaucratic development we have had here, we have seen a great deal of responsibility given to those who are not elected.
I am not going to delay matters further, Mr. Speaker, but will merely say this in conclusion. I hope I am not emphasizing too vigorously the statements that have been made by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice and agreed to by the Minister of Agriculture. Surely we do not want to provoke the United States; let us mind our own business. It seems to me that we have to wait and see what the United States are going to do in respect to many things. I can imagine some of my friends to the left-the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) who just spoke, for example-going down and asking John L. Lewis if the miners of the United States would let us reduce the taxes of the miners in Canada. No wonder, Mr. Speaker, our people are nervous. Let us be honest with ourselves and with our neighbours. Let us remove these restraints and this strangulation and get down to business. Let us

appreciate the resources we have and unloose the energy and enterprise of our people that made us so great during the war and can do the same in time of peace. Do not be fearful. There is nothing so fearful as fear itself. Nothing so certainly assures failure as to think you are going to fail.
I would urge the minister and, despite his claims and appeals last night that he had not made an error, I urge the Minister of Justice, the former Minister of Finance, to call in all the economists-they are the men who have been doctoring our economy and planning our way of life-and say to them: Let us look this situation over and see if something cannot be done; let us put a "new look" on Canadian development, put new hope into Canadian enterprise, and put a new spirit into Canadian courage and faith in ourselves. Let them say to the people of Canada: We will put an honest value on our dollar, because we know that when we put an honest value on our dollar we will improve the position of the primary producer in Canada and discourage buying in the United States; and, as a business proposition, we will put this country on an honest road to success. Give us a free dollar; give us a free market for our wheat; give us a free market for our gold; give us a free market for our products. Give us free enterprise. I say, Mr. Speaker-and I speak for myself when I say it-that I am convinced, after many years in politics, that the more strangulation, restraint and restriction you place on trade, the more you discourage enterprise, initiative and the genius that made this nation what it is.
I have no apologies to offer to my friends *who talk about state planning. They are only one degree worse in the proposals they have made than the practices of those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker. But I urge upon the one-time traditionally great Libera# party to get back, if not to the principle of laissez-faire they boasted of for fifty years, at least to free enterprise, and give us a chance to take the shackles off and be honest with ourselves.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must apologize to the hon. member who has just taken his seat. I interrupted him and told him he had exhausted his time. Unfortunately I find I made a mistake. He had seven or seven and a half minutes more.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps it is a healthy sign of the times when a large budget surplus is frowned upon in this house instead of being acclaimed; and I am sure the minister would be the first

The Budget-Mr. Quelch
to admit that very little enthusiasm was shown in this house, either on this side or on his own side, when he announced the size of the budget surplus and at the same time that there would be little or no relief from taxation. I believe the reason can be found in the concluding remarks of the minister, which will be found at page 4072 of Hansard:
Canada today enjoys a level of employment, prosperity and national income, and a standard of living and of real social security never achieved before in the history of our country.
I think the government's budget stands condemned by that statement. If it is true that today we enjoy a higher level of employment, prosperity and national income and a higher standard of living than ever before, then certainly there can be no justification for the lack of social security in this country. We have no provision for those who are physically disabled or for the aged widows; no one can feel satisfied with the very low rates of the old age pension, or the amount of money paid the recipients of the war veterans allowance. I would ask how members on the Liberal side could be enthusiastic when they know that today thousands of physically incapacitated people, many of them bedridden for years, have absolutely no provision made for them, of course apart from the blind. How can the Liberals cheer a surplus when today old age pensioners have to take a miserable pittance of anywhere from $30 to $40 a month, while recipients of war veterans allowances are tied down to the same figures? And how can we condone reducing low incomes still further by taxation, while no provision is made in the budget for increasing the exemptions?
When hon. members were discussing the menace of communism they emphasized the fact that the democracies would be at fault if they were hesitant about taking the necessary steps to prove themselves more dynamic and humanitarian than the communist countries. I have heard this budget called many names, but I have not heard anyone refer to it as a dynamic or humanitarian budget. No doubt the minister will call it a cyclical budget; and of course a cyclical budget is based upon the premise that depressions are inevitable. So in good times we tax heavily in order to reduce the national debt and also reduce the standard of living of the people and their purchasing power. In depression years we reduce taxation and increase debt, and at the same time endeavour to prevent the standard of living from falling below starvation levels.
I think all hon. members will admit that this is a rather dreary kind of roundabout, because
you never catch up with your objective. In other words, you have to wait for a war before a realistic policy is forthcoming and artificial financial limitations are modified. Then the national debt is allowed to skyrocket. After the war is over, the government once more takes it for granted that booms and depressions are inevitable, and adjusts its policies to that procedure. That has always been the record of orthodox finance. Of course, from the point of view of the usurer that may be regarded as sound finance, but from the point of view of many of the people it is a policy of despair.
If the present situation had evolved in peacetime I would agree that steps were necessary in order to prevent an inflationary rise. But the situation during the past two years has been the inevitable outcome of the war and the national financial policies of the government. That situation is rapidly changing today, due mainly to three things: the fact that people in the low-income brackets have largely spent their war savings; the fact that our loans to foreign countries have been largely spent, and the fact that reconversion in this country has been practically' completed. Our plant capacity has been greatly' increased, and either is in the process of putting forth or is about to put forth a tremendous volume of consumer goods.
Strangely enough, that situation seems to cause the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) a great deal of concern. I should like to quote what he said on this point during his budget speech, which is to be found at page 4246 of Hansard;
According to this report, a survey of some four thousand companies, 2,241 of them in operation in 1939 and 1,971 coming into operation since, shows that these companies, when alterations are completed, will have a manufacturing capacity of $8-5 billion, as against $1-8 billion in 1939. In other words, the excess over 1939 is 377 per cent. The comparable figure in the United States is fifty per cent. That is, proportionately we have gone seven and a half times as fast as the United States.
When I mentioned that the other evening the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply said: Well, what's the matter with that?-or words to that effect.
I would also interject, "What's the matter with that?" As a matter of fact, I think the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr, Howe) should be highly complimented upon the rapid progress that has been made in reconversion. Then the hon. gentleman went on;
The answer is this. If we can find markets for all these things; if we can sell all these goods and our producers of natural products can also sell all their goods, so that we will
The Budget-Mr. Quelch

capital will be provided for private investment, and we shall be able to develop our own resources instead of depending upon the United States for capital. It will tend also to stimulate venture capital in this country and will provide as well for a progressive reduction in the national debt.
W e all realize that the only way to overcome inflation and at the same time plan for a maximum standard of laving is by converting and expanding our industrial plant to a high degree of efficiency and productivity. It is true that this program in its initial stages is inflationary until the resulting flow of goods catches up to and satisfies demand. We are rapidly approaching that situation today. Obviously, if we had carried on our program of reconversion and expansion of plant more slowly, the situation would have been less inflationary. On the other hand, the sands of time are running fast and people expect today that the same vigorous action which won for us the war by high levels of production must also win for us a high standard of living in peacetime, this to be achieved as rapidly as possible.
As the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has already emphasized, we are rapidly reaching the time when a tremendous volume of consumer goods will be available to the people of Canada. This will bring an end to the inflationary pressure. I urge upon the minister the need of easing up on his anti-inflationary or deflationary policies before they land us in a position where demand lags behind supply and thus reduces our standard of living. With these facts in mind and knowing that three years after the war the people have the right to a certain basic standard of living, the hon. member for Peace River submitted certain proposals to the house as an alternative. For a moment I should like to summarize these briefly since they have been already placed on the record.
I have already placed on the record the proposal for effective control over the monetary system and a reduction of the national debt. The hon. member for Peace River proposed the following changes in expenditures in addition to the expenditures submitted by the minister. He proposed a cancellation of existing reductions in family allowances for each child after the fourth and later, as production increases, a forty per cent increase. He proposed also immediate provision for an increase in old age pensions at seventy years without a means test, with the age limit to be reduced progressively downward to sixty years as production expands.
Also pensions to needy widows of sixty years and to all disabled people not otherwise provided for; provision to increase war 
veterans allowances from $40 to $50 for single and $70 to $85 for married persons; to increase 100 per cent disability pensions to $100 a month, and the encouragement by subsidy or otherwise of the increased production of primary products the importation of which from tlm United States had caused a shortage of United States dollars. The estimated cost of those five proposals would be $289 million.
Then the hon. member proposed certain changes in revenue. He proposed that the sales tax and the twenty-five per cent excise tax be abolished, which would cost approximately $395 million. He proposed raising the exemptions for income tax for single persons from $750 to $1,500 and married persons from $1,500 to $2,400, incomes in excess of $3,000 to be taxed on a basis beginning at forty per cent. This would cost approximately $300 million. The proposed changes in corporate tax would not mean much change either way.
The total estimated loss in revenue would be $695 million; adding to that the increased expenditures of $289 million would give a total change or budget upset of $984 million. This amount to be provided for by using from the estimated surplus $484 million with a saving in interest charges of $100,000. There should be an increased revenue from remaining sources arising from taxation over and above the calculation by the minister and resulting from increased buoyancy amounting to $100 million. The remaining $300 million would be taken care of by the use of national credit. If the minister has underestimated the revenue for this year as he did last year there might very well not be any deficit at all.
In the budget debate it is permissible to-have only one amendment and one amendment to the amendment, otherwise the hon. member for Peace River would have moved his proposals as an amendment. So I shall say a few words about the two amendments that are before the house. First we have the amendment moved by the Progressive Conservative party, which is a straight vote of want of confidence. This reads:
This house is of the opinion that the government does not possess the confidence of the-country.
That of course, is just a statement of fact which I do not think anyone would dispute.. Mr. ABBOTT: Just wishful thinking.

speechtext:
You did not have a majority. The C.C.F. amendment reads:
That the said amendment be amended by inserting after the word "government" and before the word "does" in the second line of the amendment, the following words:
". . . has failed to relieve the excessive burden of taxation on the low income groups of the Canadian people:
(a)	By failing to increase the amounts of exemption from income tax from the present levels to $1,250 for single and $2,500 for married people, and . . .
The only difference there is that we feel the $1550 should be raised to $1,500. In our opinion it costs a single person more than half as much to live as it does a married couple. In many cases a single person is living in accommodation which could be used for two people. The C.CF. no doubt feel there should be some form of encouragement to get bachelors to marry, and therefore they will tax them a little bit heavier and persuade them, but we have the obvious fact that some bachelors are what one might call choosy. I do not necessarily mean to say choosy in regard to the type of female they pick up, but rather choosy with regard to the type of accommodation they want to get ready before they become married. Therefore, if you tax them too heavily they will never be in a position where they can set up house. Consequently we feel that we should reduce taxation on bachelors by raising the exemptions up to $1,500.
(b)	by failing to remove or substantially reduce the burden of sales and excise taxes which bear most heavily on those suffering from low income and the present high cost of living.
There is no question about it; we would support that.
And further, the government has failed to establish a public investment board to assure the channeling of capital investment into socially desirable projects .as a means of maintaining full employment, increasing production and raising the standard of living of the Canadian people, and . . .
We interpret full employment as meaning the full employment and development of our natural resources. With regard to the investment board, we have from time to time urged the setting up of a national monetary authority
to control the monetary system, and to bring about a proper relationship between the production of capital goods and consumer goods. We also realize that it is essential to regulate investments in the interests of the Canadian people, and prevent over-development of industries for export at the expense of the home market, and also to expand the production of these goods which at the present time we have to import from the United States, thereby draining away United States dollars. Therefore on the basis of my interpretation, we will support the C.C.F. amendment, although it does not go as far as our proposals to safeguard the welfare of the people; and furthermore, it does not provide any alternative to heavy taxation as a means of reducing our national debt.
