subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have not much to say with respect to the budget as a whole. I understand that the Minister of Finance wishes to take advantage of the prosperous years to try to reduce our debts, and I cannot object to such a sound policy.
However, I wonder whether the minister is logical in his policy in dropping the duty on cotton piece goods imported from foreign countries. The minister should know that British goods are being sold to us at prices far above the British home market. Why? I imagine it is because the Britishers want to make more money in their trading with us. In addition to that, why is it that British industry is bound to sell its goods at a cheaper price for home consumption than it does abroad? Evidently because England wants to avoid inflation at home. If this policy is good for England, I do not understand why
The Budget-Mr. L. Dionne

it should not be good for Canada. Then, how shall we control inflation in Canada if through a reduction of duty we encourage our people to buy goods from England at fancy prices? That is exactly what our people did in 1947. They bought at any price everything that appealed to them. What has happened? The government had to institute an austerity program to stop this spending spree. Any intelligent man will admit that it is not a sound policy to buy goods at prices above the market. We are no longer in a buyer's market. If the minister had got in touch with Canadian manufacturers of textiles he would have heard that we have definitely entered into a seller's market.
I know many manufacturers of textiles who have orders on hand for hardly a few weeks in advance. I know a lot of them who have a substantial amount of manufactured goods on hand, which are not sold. Mostly all Canadian manufacturers of textiles report that they receive only hand-to-mouth orders from their customers. Precisely at the time when Canadian manufacturers are preparing to undergo a severe depression in their business the minister should be very careful not to create any more undue competition. The enlargement and modernization of textile plants in Canada have been such within the last few years that the Canadian market cannot absorb our production in normal times. Canadian manufacturers are looking for export markets to keep their plants in operation. Unfortunately the sterling area seems to have created an iron curtain which does not permit goods coming from dollar countries to penetrate, namely. New Zealand, Australia, Ireland, India, British West Indies and some other countries.
I shall relate the facts to show how our export markets are gradually being closed by England. Recently a Canadian manufacturer was offered an initial order for textile goods from India, amounting to $150,000. The Canadian manufacturer accepted it. The buyer in India could not obtain a permit from his government to get the necessary dollars to pay for the goods. Why? Last year we bought $10,000,000 worth of goods from India, and we sold to India only $4,000,000 worth. There is no question of a shortage of Canadian dollars in this case. India had $6,000,000 in her favour to buy our goods. Where had the $6,000,000 gone to? The answer is England. This situation exists all over the sterling area. In such a serious circumstance I should like the minister to tell us where we shall sell our surplus of manufactured products. Shall we always be

at the mercy of England to dispose of them? If so, I can see pretty tough times ahead for the Canadian people.
Would it not be a better policy for the Minister of Finance to put his natural sympathy aside when dealing with the English people, and act like a businessman. Does the Minister of Finance imagine that the Britishers will protect our national economy? I am sure he does not; therefore, why not act accordingly?
During the war the export of textiles was forbidden by the government. A large amount of business was lost to the Canadian textile mills. On this account most of the connections that textile business had with foreign countries were disrupted. Now that the textile business is trying to regain these markets, the doors are closed by England. How long shall we have to witness our own economy being destroyed in favour of England? Are we Canadians or Britishers? This is a very serious situation, more particularly with respect to the Canadian textile industry.
The fact that Canada imported in the year 1947, 275 million yards of cotton does not prove that our Canadian industry cannot supply our markets. It only goes to show that the shelves were empty at the end of the war, and had to be replenished. The Canadian industry, which had devoted its efficiency to the production of war material, was not in a position to fill the shelves all over Canada all at one time. This explains the large volume of importations of textile goods which took place in the course of 1947, but I do not believe that all these goods are sold. A substantial quantity is still on the shelves and creates an abnormal situation for our Canadian manufacturers, because 275 million yards average over twenty-two yards for every Canadian, including babies, in addition to our own production. At present our Canadian manufacturers have to pay twenty pence to English manufacturers for synthetic fibre or rayons. The price to the English manufacturer is only sixteen pence for the same material. Before the Canadian manufacturers begin to use this English rayon, it costs them over seven cents a pound, or twenty-five per cent more than the English manufacturers.
If you compare the wages of English and Canadian labour you will note that the Canadian manufacturers have to pay at least sixty per cent more than English manufacturers to everyone of their employees. You will have the proof of this in reading the report of the Aronson wage agreement. These were British government appointed commissioners under the chairmanship of Lord

The Budget-Mr. L. Dionne
Evershed. This is a part of the agreement with reference to some textile jobs:
Per week
Picker tenders	 22.22
Strippers and card grinders	 24.00
Card tenders	 13.00
Drawing frame tenders	 16.97
Roving frame operators	 13.45
Slubbers operators	 15.76
Spinners operators	 15.76
Repair man	 22.22
Anyone can guess the enormous amount of money involved for Canadian manufacturers in this wide difference in wages.
Under such circumstances, I dare say that this drop in the duty may compel many Canadian manufacturers to reduce their production, with the result that numerous employees will be out of jobs and the national unemployment office will have to provide means of living for all of them for an indefinite period, notwithstanding the dislocation it will produce in our industry.
If English labour was not standardized; in other words, if an English employee had the right to work, to the extent of his ability and ambition, our sympathetic minister might have some kind of justification for introducing such legislation. But this is not the case. Textile plants in England are not allowed to operate on two shifts. None of these industries can operate for more than eight hours a day and no employee is allowed to perform more than a certain amount of specified work during his working time. These are the rules and regulations of the unions in England. The English businessman knows all that, but he has no control over the situation. The socialist government in England does not dare to interfere in union regulations, for reasons that everyone knows. Now our Minister of Finance indirectly asks us to support these unsound, uneconomical English labour practices to the detriment of Canadian labour.
A textile plant is so expensive that when it operates for only eight hours a day the overhead is prohibitive and the material produced in such a plant has to be sold at a very high price in order to leave a profit to the producer.
Here in Canada, labour understands this situation and in general is willing to work to the extent of its ability. Mills are operated on two shifts and sometimes three, in order to reduce the cost of the material produced in such mills.
I leave it to the house to imagine what kind of reception Canadian textile labour will give to this reduction in tariff. I do not think the Canadian Minister of Finance has any reason to take the risk of producing such a profound
disturbance in our Canadian labour for the benefit of English labour.
It should be the duty of the English government to enact proper legislation in order to enable English manufacturers to produce at a cost which will permit them to compete for foreign business.
The English government is doing exactly the contrary. Precisely when our Minister of Finance announces the drop in duty on English textile, the English government raises the price of raw cottons to British manufacturers as follows: The price of American cotton bought by the English government has been increased from 2-20 to 3-40 cents a pound. The price of Egyptian cotton has been raised 8-40 cents a pound, as published in the May 17 World Market Review of New York.
Furthermore, England is short of labour. She will naturally do as some Canadian manufacturers did last year. She will send raw cotton or synthetic fibres to be manufactured in Italy, Germany or some other country where labour is still cheaper than in Great Britain and where they are willing to work on three shifts.
The same review announces a trade pact by which England will supply raw cotton and bleached sulphite to Germany. This cotton, as well as the bleached sulphite, will be manufactured there into textile goods and filament rayon and will be shipped back to England. It involves a transaction of $55,000,000.
Broadcloth for shirts is in short supply in Canada, as well as filament rayon. We could have made the bargain direct with Germany just as well as England. We could have bought and supplied raw cotton and bleached sulphite to make cotton piece goods and filament rayon and have paid for the manufacturing of it with foodstuffs and thus begun to create a market outside of England for our agricultural products. We could thus have obtained the exact kinds of textile goods which we are short of, at a much lower price.
Unfortunately, we never thought of that. So the United States will sell cotton to England. We shall sell Canadian bleached sulphite to England. England will take a substantial profit on United States cotton and on our bleached sulphite that she will ship to Germany. England will probably pay Germany for the transformation of this raw material into any kind of textile goods with our own foodstuffs, on which she will, no doubt, make another substantial profit. She will ship us back the textile goods that she will get from Germany and again make another substantial profit on them. See how
The Budget*-Mr. L. Dionne

smart these Britishers are. How do we compare in the picture? If England cannot dispose of this $55,000,000 worth of textile goods at market price, she will dump it at any price she can get on foreign markets. She may dump it right into the Canadian market if she cannot succeed in getting the exorbitant prices she is at present asking. How can we reasonably conceive that this enormous amount of textiles will not affect our industry? How can we expect to open the doors of other countries for our textile goods under such circumstances?
Who will get the benefit of this deal? England. Who will pay for these indirect large profits and high prices? The Canadian people. Who will lose by it? The Canadian government. Who will be penalized by it? Canadian labour and the German people, who will have to accept whatever wages England decides to impose upon them.
Now, let us consider the action of the British government in regard to the German people. Here is a nation which has been living on the charity of the American people for three years. The United States wants to help put these people back on their feet and is giving away billions of dollars for this purpose. England is so managing as to make a profitable deal out of it. Is it not a pity to see the British government take advantage of American charity to exploit the misery of the starving German people?
It might be interesting for hon. members to know the national income of our people compared with the income of countries in which some of these textile piece goods will no doubt be manufactured. On referring to page 44 of congressional United States proceedings volume 4, No. 1, December 1947, I find the following information:
"The united nations conference on trade and employment now meeting in Havana, Cuba, had assembled some interesting figures on national income in terms of United States dollars," continued Mr. Javits. "The United States national income of $1,200 per person per year was probably the greatest ever attained by any people. In France, it was $300; in Great Britain, $400; in Italy and Austria, $100 and in Greece, $70 per annum. In Argentine it was $300; in Brazil, less than $100 and in Chile, about $150 per person per annum."
How do you expect our labour to compete under such conditions with labour of foreign countries where the national income is so low? The more I think of the matter, the more I am inclined to conclude that it is unfair, unjust and unwise legislation to impose on the Canadian people.
When England wants to buy something from Canada, she sends representatives here to bargain wdth us. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. 
Gardiner) knows something about the matter. My colleagues and I also remember the wheat deal of two or three years ago when England got our wheat at $1.35 to $1.55 a bushel when the market price was around $3 a bushel.
I recall the loan of $1,250 million made to England to buy our wheat. Heaven only knows if we shall ever be repaid this amount. I think the Minister of Finance has still something to learn from these Englishmen. I am practically convinced that if an English minister had the courage to propose to his government legislation such as that now submitted to us by the Canadian Minister of Finance, he would, to say the least, receive a very cold reception from his colleagues.
In proposing that cotton and rayon piece goods be admitted free in this country, the Minister of Finance states that the United Kingdom has for many years supplied an important part of our requirements of these commodities. I question this logic, because for many years England has been gradually losing her market for cotton textiles. Before the war her cotton industry was the despair of her industrialists, and her industry was unable to compete because of the labour unions' refusal to operate more than one shift. Furthermore, the labour unions opposed the introduction of automatic machinery on the ground that it would displace workers. Finally they had to admit in 1944, when they sent an official commission to the United States and Canada, that their textile industry was non-competitive. This is the handicap the English government should try to overcome. This would be a constructive and lasting move in the right direction.
The minister knows that British manufacturers sell their products at prices which are too high for us to buy. He knows these prices are very much higher than those prevailing in England. However, he is ready to let these goods come into Canada duty free. How can he justify such a strange business conception? It is simply amazing to hear such an unusual business proposition.
Does the minister think he is helping England by so doing? I dare say he is simply prolonging her agony. I know of no country, no industry and no people who can prosper without working. England will have to stop scheming and will have to abide by this universal law if she wants to get out of the rut. What England needs is to put her people to work. It is about time somebody told them that such a deal as that cannot help her. It will simply delay the greatly needed cleaning of her house. The sooner she is compelled to do it, the better for all concerned.

The Budget-Mr. Cockeram
With respect to income tax, I have already declared on two different occasions in this house that I did not favour any income tax on revenue of $1,500 for a single person and $3,000 for a married man. I do not like this method of taxation, because it is unjust, unfair and dishonest on account of the many people who evade the law. It is also a matter of great concern and anxiety for the farmers who do not know the law and who cannot comply with such legislation. How do you expect a farmer to answer properly a questionnaire such as the one printed on form T-l, a copy of which I have in my hand? It would take a competent auditor to answer intelligently every question printed on this form, and this auditor would have to follow it up year after year. Many farmers come to my office frequently with such forms asking me what to do with them. How do you want me to answer? I cannot tell them not to obey the law. On the other hand, they are unable to answer properly and intelligently practically any one of these questions. If I advise them to answer to the best of their ability, I know the income tax collectors will start to correspond with them regularly, asking for more information, until such time as the farmers get exasperated and throw the whole correspondence into the stove. Legislation should not be drafted in order to make people miserable.
I realize that the government will lose a substantial amount of revenue in exempting people with revenues of $1,500 and $3,000 respectively. But I have made suggestions to the government to compensate for this loss of revenue. I believe that if my suggestion had been given due consideration it would have helped to overcome inflation and would have been a source of satisfaction among the Canadian population.
I do not speak frequently in this house, but when I do so I try my best to co-operate in the creation of sound and honest legislation. Unfortunately, the suggestions of the backbenchers do not seem to create much of an impression on the Minister of Finance, but I hope that he will amend his ways. If he does not, we may just as well stop kidding ourselves any longer by using resounding hollow words like "autonomy", and take our colonial status which is the only rank we deserve.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In entering this budget debate, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to occupy the time of the house at any great length, but I do wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) a few pertinent facts in connection with the oppressive taxation now existent, and to make a few suggestions which I feel warrant serious consideration.
For a nation of twelve and one-half million people, our burden of taxation is excessive when considered in relationship to the stage of our development, and the problems facing us in this regard. Last year the total revenue of all governments in Canada-federal, provincial and municipal-amounted to approximately $4,058 million. This figure represents no less than 37| per cent of the national income for 1947. If w-e consider taxation from the aspect of the personal income of Canadians for 1947, which totalled $10,110 million, 40 per cent was required to maintain our various governments. By far the greater amount of this revenue, $2,819 million, was taken by the federal government.
The effect of this oppressive burden of taxation on the individual Canadian is apparently quite evident to everyone except the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the cabinet. I am sure that members who support the government in this house will agree with me in that statement.
We have come to the unfortunate position in this nation where forty cents out of every dollar of personal income last year was required to maintain our governments in the federal, provincial, and municipal fields.
One of the reasons advanced for the high percentage of personal income taken by governments in Canada is the demand for services and social security made by our people. Today in Canada, 16-2 per cent of the gross expenditures of our federal government is required to meet the costs of family allowances, old age and blind pensions, and unemployment insurance. Another 14-85 per cent of our gross expenditures goes to meet the cost of veterans' pensions. Agricultural and price control subsidies require another 4-3 per cent. Servicing of our public debt takes another 21-21 per cent. These are all charges which, in the opinion of a great many people, will in the aggregate increase rather than decrease in the years ahead.
I believe that as a democratic nation we must not only maintain but expand our social security measures in this country. As a member of this house I approve the policy of adequate pensions for those entitled to a better deal. I approve the steps which have been taken by different governments in the past in the field of social security, and recognize that the costs to the nation for social security, medical services, pensions, et cetera, will tend to increase rather than to decrease as the years go on.

The Budget-Mr. Cockeram
Last year, 8-87 per cent of our gross expenditures was required for national defence. I believe that our expenditures in this regard will tend to increase rather than to decrease in. the years that lie ahead.
With regard to national defence expenditures, I think the present program of the government is wholly inadequate and unsound. Located as we are between two countries where war hysteria is rampant-in one country because of lack of facts outside the iron curtain, and in the other country because of lack of facts inside the iron curtain-our present national defence program is wholly inadequate. We do not know whether or not Canada will be dragged into another war in the not distant future. I recognize, however, that our greatest security is preparedness, and that the Canadian people must spend money and effort to protect themselves.
I recognize, also, that we cannot build up adequate defences for this nation and at the same time lower our expenditures in this regaid, and that our defence program must necessarily be a long-range program. Unfortunately, the Russians today are obsessed by their insecurity, which leads them to believe that behind every action by the democratic nations in international affairs there must be some sinister design. As a neighbour nation of Russia, we must realize that probably generations must pass before people of that country can be expected to view the international scene with detachment, and without a feeling that every move by the outside world is designed to attack them.
Recognition of this, Mr. Speaker, should make it clear to the government and to the people of Canada that the need for us, as a nation, to build up our defences for our own security will be with us for many years and will, over those years, cost this nation vast sums of money.
In short, recognizing (a) the cost of essential services, including the servicing of our national debt; (b) the need for adequate defences for our own survival, and (c) the need for maintenance and expansion of social security measures for our people, it means that billion dollar budgets are with us to stay, as I said when I spoke on the budget last year.
I do not. however, approve the method followed by this government in meeting the costs of these things I have mentioned as essential, by the oppressive taxation with which the individual Canadian is now burdened, and which we apparently must bear until we come closer to an election. I recognize, further, that the. money has to come from somewhere, and as an alternative to this oppressive taxation I suggest a policy of expansion and development,

designed to broaden the basis of taxation and to lower the burden now carried by the Canadian people.
As a first step, I suggest the appointment of a full-time minister of mines, forests and scientific services. The action taken by the government last fall in establishing this branch of the Department of Mines and Resources was a step in the right direction, but unfortunately does not go far enough. I believe that this nation requires a full-time minister for the work now under the jurisdiction of the mines, forests and scientific services branch, and that the expenditures by this government in regard to the work of this department have been most niggardly, and penny wise and pound foolish, in the past.
With a total gross expenditure by this government last year of $2,634 million, the total expenditure to develop and assist the mineral industry of Canada was only $3,356,000. In other words, of every dollar spent by this government, approximately one-eighth of a cent was all that was spent to encourage and assist the mining industry in all its phases; and this, notwithstanding the fact that the estimated value of mineral production for 1947 was approximately $620 million, or an estimated figure of $49.60 per capita.
The mineral industry of Canada, under the able guidance and with the assistance of a fulltime minister, is capable of increasing its production to over a billion dollars annually; and if one is optimistic one can look, in the course of a few years, for an annual production in excess of the gross expenditures of this government last year.
I would suggest that the following matters of policy be taken under consideration immediately by a full-time minister of mines, forests and scientific services:
1. Decide with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) what is to be the policy of this nation in regard to the processing in Canada of primary mineral products, giving due regard to domestic demand and ability to sell in foreign markets.
2.	Review with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) our present position with regard to existing supplies of strategic minerals both from a domestic and a continental defence aspect. It is no secret that dangerous shortages of strategic minerals exist in the United States today, particularly in regard to lead, zinc, copper, high-grade iron ore, and petroleum, and I would be most surprised if similar conditions do not prevail in Canada at the present time.
3.	Review with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) anticipated demands for employ-

The Budget-Mr. Argue
ment in Canada-a problem which could quite conceivably become a matter of urgent national importance.
It is recognized that for every man in Canada employed underground in the mining industry, employment is provided for ten other people in servicing the demands of the industry in various fields.
4.	Review with the minister of immigration the ability of the industry to absorb, in gainful employment, above Canadian demands, those who come to this country from abroad in search of a new home and a new life.
5.	Reconsider the question of assistance to the provinces to defray the costs of improving transportation facilities into mining areas discontinued by this government last year.
This work in the past has had the effect of encouraging active development in many promising areas hitherto devoid of transportation facilities. I refer more particularly to the Snow lake district in northern Manitoba and to the Yellowknife district of the Northwest Territories.
6.	Provide for scientific technical and other investigations designed to further the development of the mining, metallurgical and related industries in Canada and the production of commercial products from otherwise waste materials.
7.	Provide greater governmental research facilities for the purpose of discovering greater efficiency in lower mining costs, and greater recovery from ores at present available.
8.	As mineral production increases, and since minerals are a wasting asset, I suggest that such a program is essential and that a greater appropriation should be made for geological survey work than has been provided for in the past.
9.	Reverse the present policy of the bureaucrats behind the government of this country, and take immediate steps to develop among Canadians an appreciation of the economic importance of the mining industry to this nation.
I believe that these suggestions warrant serious consideration by this government. True, they involve expenditures beyond those at present provided; but they are expenditures which will be repaid many times over in increased production, increased employment, increased revenue to the government in the way of taxes, and, last but not least, increased security for this nation.
All parties in this house are in accord with the principle of budgeting for a surplus of revenues over expenditures. But we are not in agreement with such a policy at the expense of:
1. Oppressive taxation on lower incomes.
2.	Paying off a large proportion of war debts by the present generation without corresponding governmental assistance to facilitate making the natural resources of this country available to the present generation to meet these heavy taxes.
3.	Without any appreciable effort on behalf of the government to curtail and eliminate waste and extravagance.
It is significant that in the presentation of his budget the Minister of Finance failed to give concrete evidence of any real effort by his department and other government departments to eradicate duplication, waste and extravagance.
I listened with particular interest to the speech delivered this afternoon by my good friend the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). The hon. member recalled the statement made eighteen years ago when, in the face of the Hawley-Smoot tariff, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) urged parliament and the people of Canada to frame our tariff policies so as not in any case to provoke the United States. He recalled the words of the Minister of Finance uttered in this house six months ago that we must tax Canadian industries twenty-five per cent so as to protect the long-range interests of United States firms.
Last night we heard from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) speaking for the government and telling the house that before tax reductions are considered in this house we must conduct ourselves so that we shall not be "severely criticized and penalized by the United States".
In the words of a member of the press gallery, the budget was written "by the uneasy light of the stars in fear of the stripes".

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when introducing the budget the minister gave us a summary of world conditions today. In my opinion, and I believe it is all to the good, the war hysteria which was so rampant in Canada some months ago has now ebbed considerably. I believe that only through working in the united nations with the other great countries can Canada do her part toward bringing about peace and prosperity in the world.
I am sorry that the government has not yet seen fit to recognize the new state of Israel. Our Canadian delegation supported the partition of Palestine. It seems to me that partition is now a fact, and our government should follow the governments of the United States, the U.S.S.R., and now our sister commonwealth nation, the Union of South Africa, in recognizing this state of Israel, so that Jewish people throughout the world may have in fact their long-hoped-for national home.
The Budget-Mr. Argue

It has been said often in this debate that the Canadian people were disappointed by this budget. That is putting it mildly. The Canadian people generally expected more from the government. They expected more, because the government has said to them during the war and also during the 1945 election, "If .you elect us we will prevent inflation, we will provide stability of prices and we will implement with the provinces an over-all social security program." So the people of Canada were disappointed. When, on the one hand, they saw a large surplus of revenues over expenditures, namely $670 million, and at the same time they saw in the budget no real evidence that the government was prepared to improve the lot of the average working man, they were disappointed.
In my opinion the government in this budget has done nothing to improve the lot of the average Canadian. Moreover, the lot of the average Canadian has worsened considerably since the budget of 1947, as a result of government policy. The people of Canada at this time were hoping that the eight per cent sales tax would be removed, that exemptions from income tax would be increased and that the government would undertake a social security program to provide better and more adequate old age pensions, and to provide an over-all health program.
There are many people in Canada at the same time-a growing number-who in a sense are not disappointed in the budget because they could not expect much from this government. I refer to the rank and file membership of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation. The C.C.F. has become a national party because it believes that the present free enterprise system of the Liberal government, or any alternative free enterprise government, will not and cannot bring forward the legislation that is necessary to provide all Canadians with a decent standard of living and a fair share of the great wealth Canada can produce.
The members of the C.C.F. party across Canada know that their party has an alternative to the present inadequate, reactionary and backward-looking budget. The C.C.F. record is clear. It stands for price control; it stands for the removal of the sales tax on the necessities of life; it stands for a national labour code with adequate minimum wages and with a work week of forty hours. The C.C.F. party believes that profits of corporations should be kept within reason. Profits should not be allowed to run wild until they reach the point where, as the minister emphasized in his budget speech time and time again, capital expansion on
[Hr. Argue.]
construction and equipment reaches the stage where it adds severely to the inflationary spiraling of prices. The C.C.F. party believes that the only way to handle the great monopolistic corporations which so dominate the economic life of the Canadian people today is to bring those corporations under public ownership and operate them for the benefit of the Canadian people at large.
Canadians did not expect that in May, 1948, three years after the war, the cost of living would be as high as it is. Canadians did not expect to see inflation rampant in this country. At one time the minister prophesied that he expected the cost of living index would settle around 145, but today it is 152. The Ottawa Citizen of January 16 contained an article giving statements by various members of government made during the past few years in relation to the problem of inflation and price control. The statement is headed in this way-

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was about to deal with some of the commitments made by members of the government to the people of Canada, namely, that the government in the post-war period would undertake such measures as would prevent inflation. I was about to quote from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of January 16, 1948. The first part of the article reads as follows:
During the past seven years federal cabinet ministers and officials have been giving warning of the evils of inflation and high prices in announcing their determination to guard the Canadian people from them. At a time when inflation threatens to become acute through the abandonment of controls and subsidies, the following quotations make interesting reading.
J. L. Usley, May, 1945:
"Sharply rising prices in -the demobilization and reconversion period would undoubtedly be followed by deflation and serious unemployment afterward. Stable prices are therefore essential so that there may be a smooth adjustment to peacetime economy."
Annual Report of Bank of Canada for fiscal year ending March 31, 1947:
"Any excessive run-up in prices and costs would set the stage for subsequent deflation. It would affect different economic groups very un-

The Budget-Mr. Argue
equally and the resulting distortions would necessitate fresh adjustments before the basis would exist for a balanced and stable prosperity."
Mr. Abbott, Minister of Finance, January 11, 1947:
"A further orderly removal of emergency controls becomes effective on January 13, 1947. It is part of a deliberate and carefully-considered plan, designed to eliminate war-imposed restrictions as promptly as is consistent with the prevention of the sort of boom and collapse in prices -which was typical of developments after the first world war. The goal of the government's stabilization policy has always been and still is to preserve orderly conditions with a view to cutting off the disrupting peak in postwar prices and to avoiding, or at least greatly lessening, the drop which inevitably follows.
Throughout the past seven years, the government has committed itself to an anti-inflationary policy. Through many statements of ministers and officials the government has promised that price controls would be abandoned only after the danger of inflation no longer existed. Events during the past twelve months prove beyond the shadow of a doubt that the government has not kept its commitment to the Canadian people. Instead, it has removed price controls until today the cost of living is so high that the average Canadian finds it difficult to purchase the necessities of life from the shrinking value of his dollar.
In 1946 the increase in the cost of living index over 1945 was only 4 points. Throughout that time controls were maintained; but from February, 1947, to February, 1948, the cost of living increased by 22 points; an increase of only 4 points when the government was maintaining general price controls, with subsidies, and an increase of 22 points when the government abandoned its own program of price controls. So bad had the inflation situation become that the government found it necessary to do something to relieve itself from the attack of the Canadian people upon its price decontrol policy. And so the government set up a committee of the House of Commons to inquire into prices. Members of Parliament well know that, even since that committee has been set up, prices have continued to rise. Not one thing has come out of that committee that is known to have reduced the prices of any important commodities. In my opinion, by setting up the prices committee the government was merely trying to relieve itself from the justifiable wrath of the Canadian people. That committee has turned out to be nothing less than a whitewash, a poor substitute for the government's once good price control policy.
In his budget speech the minister repeated time and time again that one of the main
causes of the increase in prices was that corporations were expanding too rapidly in the field of reconstruction and in equipment replacement.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You mean, employment was too high?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, don't be ridiculous. I am merely quoting back to you what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has told the house. My hon. friend, being a good independent Liberal, should accept the minister's word for it, as I do. However, Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement bears out the belief of the members of this group that the great financial interests in Canada should be nationalized. If they were placed under the control of parliament those policies could be inaugurated which would channel investments into such industries as at this time would increase the quantity of consumer goods available to the people of Canada.
Throughout the last year members of this group have from time to time quoted figures of various corporations, showing that profits have reached an all-time unprecedented high. When members of this group did that there was a general pooh-pooh from members opposite, who stated that we were merely selecting a few corporations and then making a broad, sweeping statement that all profits had risen accordingly. However, the figures presented in the white paper prove that the great corporations of Canada are making the highest profits in their history. What the Canadian people wish to know is how they as individuals have been taken care of through government policy as compared with the giant corporations.
On December 31 last, the government removed the excess profits tax. That tax on excess profits in the fiscal year 1945-46 yielded the government revenues of approximately $494 million, and in 1946-47, $448 million. These revenues will no longer be obtained because the government has removed the excess profits tax. I believe that tax was a fair tax; it was a just tax; it was a tax on excess earnings, and surely the companies that make excess earnings could better afford to pay taxes to the national exchequer than a single man earning something more than $750 or a married man struggling along on something over $1,500 a year.
The figures in the white paper prove beyond the Shadow of a doubt that within the last twelve months corporation income has increased much faster than the income of the Canadian people. Corporation income in 1946 amounted to $1,421 million; in 1947 it was
The Budget-Mr. Argue

$1,821 million. That was an increase of twenty-eight per cent. In the white paper the government tells us that personal incomes increased by only seven per cent, so that the profits of big corporations increased in 1947 over 1946 by an amount four times as great as the increase in the personal income of Canadians.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where do you get your figures?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Out of the government's white paper.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am studying it now and I cannot see that.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Read it carefully and you will find out. Corporation profits after taxes amounted in 1946 to $751 million and in 1947 to $1,017 million, or an increase of thirty-five per cent. That is corporation profits after taxes. Individual incomes, after direct taxes, increased from $704 per capita in 1946 to $741 per capita in 1947, or an increase of five per cent. So that the sum available to business, after paying taxes in 1947, had increased by an amount five times as much as the income of individual Canadians.
That, I submit, shows beyond contradiction that the government's policy within the last year has been one to make certain that the profits of big business in Canada increased to a far greater extent than wages, salaries and incomes of Canadians generally.
The cost of living index in February, 1948, as compared with February, 1947, had increased by seventeen per cent. During that period, personal incomes of Canadians had increased by only five per cent. The cost of living index had gone up by seventeen per cent, and individual incomes had gone up by only five per cent, so that the average Canadian in 1947 had twelve per cent less real income than he had in 1946.
I now come to undistributed profits of corporations, or, in other words, savings of corporations. In 1946 undistributed profits amounted to $411 million, and in 1947, to $609 million, an increase of $198 million, or forty-eight per cent. But individual Canadians within that period were unable to save at the same rate that they had previously, so that we find personal savings of individuals in 1946 were $957 million, and in 1947 those individual savings had shrunk to $588 million, a reduction of $369 million, or thirty-eight per cent. Undistributed profits increased by forty-eight per cent, but the savings of Canadians decreased by thirty-eight per cent.
In a situation such as that, one would expect that any government that had the interests of
(Mr. Argue.]
the Canadian people at heart would increase the taxes of big business and decrease the taxes of individual Canadians. But on page 4061 of Hansard, in his budget speech the minister estimates that corporation taxation in 1948-49 will be $591 million as compared with total corporation taxes of $687 million in 1947-48, or a reduction in the amount of tax levied on corporations to the extent of $96 million.
Personal income taxes, the minister estimates, will produce $15 million more revenue in 1948-49 than in 1947-48, so that, in spite of the fact that corporations have increased profits tremendously, in spite of the fact that the average Canadian cannot save as much as he did a year ago, the government in this budget is reducing taxes on corporations by $96 million and expects to extract $15 million more in personal income taxes from individual Canadians.
The minister, on page 4056 of Hansard, in the budget speech, says:
As consumers, -we are bidding eagerly for a limited supply of goods, throwing into the auction not only most of our current incomes but also part of our past savings and additional funds obtained by instalment credit.
He is saying that the individual Canadian is now throwing into the auction most of his present income and part of his past savings and is going into debt. In other words, the average Canadian is going bankrupt today at a time when big business is making large, unprecedented and unjustifiable profits.
The minister last year, in his budget, which foretold the removal of excess profits tax, which foretold his policy of removing price control, made the following statement on page 2626 of Hansard:
With the orderly removal of controls, with increasing supplies of material, with efficient and co-operative labour, and with ample markets, Canadian business enterprise is in a most favourable situation. We all expect it to show its mettle, both in production and in marketing.
Then note this:
We expect it to show its ability to keep down costs and prices. In its own long-run interest, as well as in the national interest, business must keep its prices down and its profits writhin reason.
The minister last year placed his hope in business. He said that in its own interest business must keep its prices down, but business did not keep its prices down. Prices have gone up tremendously, and still, in spite of the fact that big business had not warranted the faith the minister last year placed in it, the minister in his budget this year is doing nothing about the matter.
Does the minister think an increase in corporation profits of twenty-eight per cent is

The Budget-Mr. Argue
keeping profits within reason? Does he think an increase of thirty-five per cent in corporation profits, after taxes, is keeping profits within reason? Does he think an increase in undistributed profits in one year of forty-eight per cent is keeping profits within reason?
The members of the C.C.F. group believe that these profits are far too high. We believe that corporation taxation should be increased. If the government did that, they could get hundreds of millions of dollars of additional revenue, and at the same time they would slow down the huge capita;! expansion program which the minister has said is a factor causing much of the present day inflation. But after last year, when events have shown that the minister's faith in business was not justified, he states this year, on page 4056 of Hansard:
The policy of the government has been to return to a free price system and to moderate the inevitable increases in prices at this time by whatever fiscal and other methods are possible under such a system.
The minister this year tells the house that increases in prices are inevitable. But last year he was telling business to show its mettle, and to keep its prices and costs down.
Then we come to the changes outlined in the budget. One of the changes was to increase the tax exemption for a married couple over sixty-five years of age. Last year a married couple earning $2,000 paid an income tax of $70. This year they will not have to pay any income tax at all. The people in Canada over the age of sixty-five who last year had a net income of $1,930 will this year be given an additional income of $70 to bring their income up to $2,000. But the old age pensioners, the couple who are living on $60 a month, or $720 a year, are getting nothing from this budget.

speechtext: That is not so in British Columbia.

I think it would have been much better had those changes not been made and had that
$10,000,000 been spent on the old age pensioners today. There were 210,000 old age pensioners in Canada in 1947. That $10,000,000 would have meant an additional $48 per pensioner per annum, or an increase of $4 a month.
