subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why are they moving out to British Columbia?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Keep on asking questions.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think it is a crime that throughout the budget the various changes made by the minister mean that the people in Canada who have already received or are receiving a high income will get a higher income while those people who are struggling along on a low income will get no benefits from this budget.
The C.C.F. group believe in better old age pensions. The government has led the Canadian people to believe, through its proposals to the provinces, that a general old age pension would be paid to everyone at seventy years of age, without a means test; and that the federal government would make a fifty per cent contribution available to the provinces for the pensions of people between the ages of sixty-five and seventy. But the government has not done that. The Liberal government had not provided the social security legislation that the Canadian people were looking for.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And British Columbia pays for it.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the government took care of the security needs of some Canadians. In 1947, this government introduced a bill, and passed it in spite of C.C.F. opposition, which increased the salary of the leader of the government in the other place by $7,000, giving him a total salary of $13,000.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about our own increase?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Was that a salary or a pension?
The Budget-Mr. Argue

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have heard it called an "old man's home"; but when I hear of a salary of $13,000, it seems to me to be a pretty good home.
The same government in 1946 presented and passed in this house a bill to increase by one-third the salaries of judges. The government said, with regard to a judge who had been receiving $16,000, that for him to be a good judge, he must have a good income; and that $15,000 a year was not enough for a judge. So the government said, "We will give him $20,000 a year and we will give the old age pensioners $30 a month."

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did we not study law?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The C.C.F. party does not agree with a policy of that kind.
Then there was the famous pension for the members of the diplomatic service. The government guaranteed them a pension of from $3,000 to $7,000 a year, even if they had been in the diplomatic service for a period of only five years.
The government, in its proposals to the Canadian people in 1945, stated that it was prepared to assume sixty per cent of the national health insurance program. It estimated at that time that that sixty per cent would cost the federal treasury $150 million a year. The government did nothing for a long time after the 1945 election. A few weeks ago it announced proposals whereby the provinces could obtain, through various steps, up to $30 million a year. The federal government in 1945 promised the Canadian people $150 million a year for better health services. It waited for three years and then brought in a scheme to provide only $30 million a year. In this regard, Mr. Speaker, the government has kept its promise to the extent of only twenty per cent.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think I should end my speech on the budget without emphasizing the problems that face farmers at the present time. I can remember that ten years ago tractor gasoline could be bought for sixteen cents a gallon. That same gasoline todays costs thirty cents a gallon. Combines have gone up until now one of the better combines-a 14-foot self-propelled combine

will cost $5,000. The fanners beieve that their machinery is costing from two to three times as much as its value. Imperial Oil profits for 1947 were over $3,000,000 higher than in 1946. Massey-Harris profits in 1947 were almost fifty per cent more than in 1946. The Cockshutt Plow Company profits had increased by fifty per cent. The
[Mr. Gibson (Comox-Al'bernd) .1
Canadian Pacific Railway Company in applying for an increase in freight rates, estimated that its net railway income in 1947 would be $14,800,000. Instead of that, its net railway income turned out to be $22,800,000, or $8,000,000 more than it had estimated.
The picture across Canada is the same for almost all other corporations. Profits are going up by leaps and bounds. Companies can now charge everything the traffic will bear. The packing industry has told us that it charges the highest prices it can obtain for its products and that it buys the farmers' produce at the lowest possible prices.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Good old free enterprise.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The record of the Liberal
government today shows that, in all its major legislation, it has increased the profits of big business. It is increasing the net income of certain individuals over sixty-five years of age who are now earning $2,000 a year or more. At the same time it has not increased the old age pension. It is paying higher salaries and pensions to people in the other chamber, to judges and to tired diplomats, and at the same time this government is allowing prices to go sky-high, until today the average consumer in Canada does not know where he will get the money to buy an adequate supply of food and proper clothing, to educate his family, and to pay for a decent home. It is time the government changed its program.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Change the
government.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will leave that to the Canadian people. Some seventy-six per cent of the Canadian people believe in price control, and I think it fair to assume that seventy-six per cent do not believe in the government opposite.
The Canadian people would like to see the following changes made at this time:
1.	Reimpose price controls on essential commodities and reinstate subsidies on essential goods.
2.	Increase corporation taxes and reinstate the excess profits tax.
3.	Raise the income tax exemptions to at least $1,250 for a single man and $2,500 for a married couple.
4.	Socialize the chartered banks so that loans may de directed in such a way as to increase the production of consumer goods.
5.	Increase old age pensions to $50 at the age of sixty-five, without a means test.
6.	Implement a national prepaid health service program.
7.	Levy the farmers' income tax in a fair and equitable manner; and this is important if we are to get the production we need.

The Budget-Mr. D. G. Ross
8.	Remove the unjust twenty-one per cent increase in freight rates; and I wish to emphasize that the increase in freight rates is a most important issue in the west at this time.
Mr. DOUGLAS G. ROSS (St. Paul's): Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat says the socialists advocate an increase in the corporation tax. I wonder if he realizes, and if he does not I should like to point out to him, that the corporation tax now collected by the government is figured in the cost of doing business, so that to increase the corporation tax would mean that the products of business would have to go up in price.
In taking part in this debate I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on the way he brought down his budget on Tuesday, May 18, the budget to which all the people of Canada had been looking forward with high hopes for so long. The people of Canada expected some relief from taxation as a result of information which had been given out with respect to the surplus we were to have at the end of the year; but they were sadly disappointed. With the exception of one or two features, this budget was a disappointing document. It marks a departure from sound principles of taxation.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that in 1946 the government budgeted for a deficit of 8300 million and showed a surplus of $374 million. In other words, it took in $674 million more than it budgeted for. This may have been an error in judgment, but believe me it was some error. Again in 1947 the government budgeted for a surplus of $190 million and turned up with a surplus of $670 million, a miscalculation amounting to the huge sum of $480 million. In the two years the miscalculation in its forecasts amounted to only $1,054 million. These miscalculations must come as a bit of a shock to many people. It may be a pleasant shock, but just the same it is a shock.
I cannot think they were altogether errors in judgment; they were too large. Even taking into consideration the immensity of the calculations necessary in preparing a budget, it seems to me that a more accurate forecast could have been made. The government had all the information at its disposal; it had the experience of the 1946 forecast, and the actual results that year. I cannot help thinking-and many others feel the same.-that it was either the result of a combination of guesswork and incompetency, or deliberately arrived at for some ulterior motive. Perhaps the government felt it would Like to prepare for an early general election this year, and wanted' to turn up with a surplus of $670 million in order to 5849-284
show the people of Canada what fine fellows they were. It can be fairly assumed that mistakes and errors of judgment are to be anticipated, but surely not on this scale.
As I said before, the surplus was anticipated by the public from at least the middle of the year, according to the information they had been given. In fact they thought it would be closer to a billion dollars; and certainly they thought there would be a substantial easing of taxation in the various fields. What a let-down the people have had 1 They have been given practically no relief. This year taxes are proposed not only to provide for expenditures but for the sum of $549,000,000 in excess of requirements, the largest amount ever budgeted for in the history of Canada. Apparently one of the objectives is to cut down expenditure by taxpayers with a view to guarding against inflation. This is not a taxation principle; it is but an extension of the controls which most people wished to have diminished as rapidly as possible following the war and finally done away with. This country has been built up and has prospered largely through the thrift and enterprise of its people. I am sure- it would be better and safer to depend upon the thrift of the individuals than to take all available money away from them in order to prosecute plans which may not be quite so successful as the planners hope. I believe the people of Canada want to provide for themselves with as little government aid as possible.
It always happens that one control leads to another, and results in an increase in the cost of living. Taxation comes out of all the people, not just a few. The people in the middle brackets are just about as hard hit as anyone. It is very difficult for them to get on with the high rates of taxation in effect at the present time.
The minister tried to point out that the government was exercising every possible economy. It does not seem to me like that. If one looks at the estimated expenditures he will find that the onlv economy contemplated is to be imposed on the taxpayers of Canada. While in 1939 we had
49,000	civil servants, today we have 117,000, all of whom are non-productive.
I would point out that for every thousand millions dollars by which we reduce our debt, we reduce our interest charges by about $27,000,000. Let me point this out, that for every ten thousand civil servants we are able to do without today-and if the government would use better methods of economy, I
The Budget-Mr. D. G. Ross

believe we could do without many of them- we would make a saving of at least $20,000,000 to the taxpayers of Canada.
Going through the estimates, we find that in the ordinary expenditures there is an increase this year of more than 8174,000,000- an increase, in this day and age, over last year. That is in the main estimate. It is right there, on ordinary expenditures. Certainly this does mot look like vigilance on the part of the government in reducing expenditures. I say there should have been a reduction instead of an increase in these ordinary expenditures.
And, by the way, I should like to quote an article that appeared in today's Ottawa Journal, which states:
There is another line of attack parliament might take 'and more usefully. Attack upon expenditures.
It goes on to say:
Increased expenditures since 1938 due to the war total $831,753,373. Increased expenditures since 1938, not due to the war, total $737,681,383.
And then the Journal goes on to say:
Here is Parliament's real job. The job of watching what the government does with the great surpluses it has on hand, land will have on hand; checking the temptation to spend which will be born of such great sums of money.
And it goes on to say:
The checking of estimates, with audit of accounts, is parliament's traditional function. Parliament has been betraying that function.
The article states that is one reason why taxes are high and expenditures are high. That is true. Some method will have to be taken by parliament to check on these expenditures.
It will be noticed that when the estimates are under consideration it is very difficult to get any detailed information on expenditures. For the average member of parliament it is impossible to get from the ministry any details with respect to expenditures. Ministers should be able to give that information. Surely there is some way of getting it, some way in which the ministers of each department could be questioned-in a committee, or in some other way.
For instance, in this year we shall find that hundreds of millions of dollars will be put through before the end of June. There has been much talk about one thing and another; but the real business of parliament is to get down to the matter of seeing that expenditures in this country are kept down, and to see that the government is not overspending.
As I said before, in 1946 there was a reduction in taxes with a budget forecast deficit of

S300 million. This reduction was hardly expected, but it came. It is true that when the $374 million surplus was announced in 1947, after the year's operations, the people expected an easement of taxes, and they got it. Now, with an estimated surplus of $549 million for 1948-49 and a surplus of $374 million in 1946 and $670 million in 1947 there is practically no relief for the taxpayer of Canada.
I want to say, no matter what anyone else says, that the people of Canada are good and mad because they have not had some relief from taxation. It is all very well and most commendable to reduce the debt, but in reasonable amounts. In 1946 the net debt rvas $13,421 million; in 1947 it was $13,069 million, or a reduction of $352 million. In 1948 the net debt was $12,377 million, or a further reduction of $692 million; or a total reduction in two years of $1,044 million, or eight per cent.
People certainly expected they would be given some relief by way of a reduction in taxation. Also I am sure they expected there would be some debt reduction as well. Might I say in passing that there are many more thousands, if not millions, of people needed in Canada to help develop this country, to produce and to work out their living for themselves on their own behalf. The more we have here, the fewer we shall have to feed overseas. The more we have here, the more we shall have to help feed those who are overseas. The more we have here, the more we shall have to help service our $12,377 million debt.
Now, what about the estimated surplus of $549 million for 1948-49? With the example of the 1946 forecast, which was underestimated to the extent of $647 million; and with the 1947 underestimation of $670 million, how accurate is the 1948 calculation? Should it be $800 million, $900 million or $1,000 million?
In any event, the mounting cost of living is not underestimated. Under present government policy it may be expected that the cost of living will continue to rise. It has risen in Canada from an index of 131 in April, 1947, to an index of 152 in April of this year, or an increase of 21 points. The cost of clothing has gone up 36 points. It will probably approach the cost of living index in the United States index of 168. The cost of living in the United States has risen by only 12 points in the year. If this occurs-and it probably will-revenues will increase rapidly. Everything points to a much larger surplus, and also everything points to an election next year.

The Budget-Mr. D. G. Boss
I do not know whether the minister has deliberately underestimated, for the purposes of an election next year. I cannot say that definitely. But, judging from his budget, I would suggest that this might be so. And what a hurrah there will be when the election is called-when the government is deader than it is now. It will have to have artificial life from somewhere. The public will have to have some kind of shot in the arm in order to keep them sweet with the government. I suppose that shot in the arm from the government will be a huge surplus and huge tax cuts. I cannot say that will happen, but I am bound to forecast that I believe it may happen, and I shall be more accurate than the minister.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), speaking in the house on Wednesday, said that this kind of budget does not provoke immediate commendation. Indeed it does not-it has provoked condemnation. He said that it will get more approval as time goes on, but he does not need to fool himself. The people do not like to be mulcted for political reasons under any guise or excuse, but that is what they think this government is doing. It is a bid for power next year, but they will not forget.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) referred to what the Minister of Justice had given as a reason for there being no reduction in taxation this year, that because of the tremendous efforts the United States people are putting forth by way of aid to Europe we could not do much more than we are doing; they would resent our shoving our taxes down. What utter nonsense!
Let me point out that Canada has done more in this connection on a per capita basis than has the United States. Despite the tables in Hansard with regard to federal and state income taxes, the people of Canada are paying far more than are the people in the United States when we take into consideration sales and excise taxes and customs duties. The people of Canada have nothing to be ashamed of, nor need they make excuses to their friends to the south even if our taxes were lowered. I would also point out that we in Canada are paying for two years more of war than are the people of the United States. So no reduction of taxes because they might be annoyed! In the meantime the people are mulcted of their hard-earned wages.
As I said before, the public expected an easement of taxation. Only last week when I was home in Toronto, several office managers informed me that a day or so after the budget was announced employees began flocking to their offices requesting wage increases. These increases are asked because the government's
5849-284J
inflationary policy has increased the cost of living. Increased wages will increase costs, further adding to inflation.
Because of taxes-personal income tax, sales tax and excise tax on soft drinks, candy, cigarettes, et cetera-the average man finds it most difficult to put anything aside. His income is exhausted by taxation and current bills. Wage earners seek relief from the high cost of living by demanding more take-home pay. Without there being some reduction in taxation, that is bound to happen.
What about the eight per cent sales tax? The eighty cents that was paid by way of tax on an article which sold for $10 wholesale in 1939, in most cases, because of the increased price of the article, is now $1.20, $1.40 or even $1.60. Hon. members can see how inflationary that is. It tends to hamper and discourage the production of goods. Production is the real cure for inflation. As I pointed out, even with the present level of the corporation tax, part of the cost of doing business is such that the selling price of manufactured articles must be increased.
Let us consider the inexcusable and iniquitous excise tax of twenty-five per cent. In many cases this tax is imposed upon the retail price which includes the sales tax. Also take the tax on automobiles as another example. The cheapest car on the market sells for $1,655 retail. The excise tax on this car is $256; the sales tax is $82.20, or a total tax of $328. The mark-up of twenty per cent on these taxes amounts to $67, making a total increased cost of $405 to the buyer. Automobiles of this type are not luxuries. There is no more room in the large cities and people have to go to the suburbs. A car is a necessity because the hard pressed man has to get out of the city. But he finds that he must pay $405 more. That is inflation; you cannot get away from it.
All these taxes are being left on with this budget to obtain an advantageous position next year in the case of a general election. The minister says the government is unwilling to lighten the burden of taxation because of its policy of fighting inflation with taxes or, in other words, the planned control of spending. He terms this policy anti-infiationary, but that is a misnomer.
Taxation in this country has aggravated inflationary tendencies because it is too onerous and unjudiciously applied. What has happened? Bank statements show that the rate of public saving has dropped because of the rising cost of living as expressed in the wholly fallacious price index for consumer goods and the heavy impost on personal earnings. The desire to save and the pride of ownership have to a great degree been destroyed. As a matter of fact,
The Budget-Mr. D. G. Ross

they have been made impossible because of these taxes. It is not only those in the low-income brackets who are having a bad time; those in the middle income brackets are having just as tough a time.
As I said, the budget is inflationary because the present taxation brings savings out of the bank or out of the old sock. It tends to liquidate savings in bonds and discourages investment in productive enterprise and thus hinders production. The collection of so much money by taxation tends toward improvident spending on the part of the government. It draws money out of productive employment and spends it on an overlarge army of government employees and bureaucrats, most of w'hom are non-productive, as well as pumping the money back into consumer channels by way of salaries and wages, with no production of real wealth.
If there ever was a policy which was not anti-inflationary, the policy of this government is certainly one. Talk about controls; one control just leads to another and you never know where you are going to end. It is just about as hard to control individual spending without inflation.
Then, as to the government policy with respect to importations from Great Britain, the minister is reported on page 4063 of Hansard as follows:
If we diverted our prospective surplus into a redutetion of taxes now, it would add hundreds of millions of dollars 'a year to the already intense demand of Canadians for goods and services-
I doubt that very much.
-but it would add nothing to the volume of Canadian goods and services available for sale. People would try to buy more, but there would not be more to buy, unless tbe effort to get it resulted in more. imports that we cannot afford and which we would have to shut out somehow or other. Prices would be sure to rise.
Unless it resulted in more imports that we cannot afford to buy. There are imports from Great Britain which we can afford to buy. In fact it is most necessary to do so. We have a staggering but stagnant balance with them now. We all know that Great Britain needs goods and foodstuffs from Canada. London will have to dip into her dollar and gold reserves to the tune of $1 billion for the year ending December. It shows that they do need the money. We must do everything we possibly can to see that they get the money. Canada can produce the food that Great Britain needs, but Britain needs the cash to buy these goods. This government is taxing the people at the present time to buy from themselves to send to Britain; in other words, we are lifting ourselves by our bootstraps,

creating a false prosperity. We have that right here at the present time. We are selling to Great Britain for no productive return. Quality and quantity of goods on the market are the best things in the world to stop inflation.
This policy is having only one effect, augmenting and emphasizing the impact of scarcity of consumer goods in Canada, and further increasing inflation. The government is hoping that the Marshall plan, the ERP program, will have some effect and will save Canada from its present dilemma. I think the government's hopes are groundless, if we may judge from the information we get on the condition of the countries over there. In the meantime the government has prohibited the importation of certain goods and placed other goods under quotas and import controls in the austerity program. That is inflation. It prevents the goods from coming in; therefore it increases prices. This program is, of course, government control in Canada-with a vengeance.
Great Britain comes under the same category as that of the United States in this program. Why should this be? Why should Great Britain be placed in the same category, when she needs our funds and our goods? I suggest that all these controls against the importation of goods from Great Britain be done away with at once. There are many hundreds of products of the British isles which could come in here in normal trade. It would be encouraging to the people of Great Britain. The suspension of the preferential tariff on British cottons and rayon goods is to be commended. Remove all the articles, or most of them, from schedule I, the prohibited list and it will increase the supply of goods in Canada and be anti-inflationary. It will help Britain and Canada.
The reduction of taxes, combined with the supplementing of supplies from Great Britain, will aid in reducing prices and combating inflation. The plans of 'the planners have gone wrong. They have not stopped inflation in prices or reduced the cost of living. Taxes have a great bearing on it. The government must cut down on its expenditures and get away from so much paternalism and regimentation, and the control over the spending of the people. The people want to stand on their own feet. They want an opportunity to make their own way in this wonderful country of ours, to use their own initiative and to spend and save their own money according to their better judgment. I ask the government and the parliament of Canada to trust the people.

The Budget-Mr. Maclnms
Mr. ANGUS MaeINNIS (Vancouver East): Mr. Speaker, the best that one can say of this budget is that its sins are sins of omission rather than of commission. It is indeed the kind of budget that one would expect from a bright young Conservative lawyer called to administer an important government department. If I may be allowed to paraphrase a famous statement I would say of this budget that seldom did a finance minister say so little in so many words; nevertheless there are a few items in it that deserve analysis.
I wish to refer for a few moments to the raising of the income tax exemptions on incomes of persons sixty-five years of age and over. There are valid reasons for raising income tax exemptions at this time, but surely it should be done on the basis of income and not on the basis of age. This is adopting a new principle in Canadian taxation, and may I say it is a most illogical principle. If it is carried to its logical conclusion, some day when you give your little boy eight cents to go to the store to buy a chocolate bar the person behind the counter will ask him, "Is it for yourself or for your grandmother?" That is exactly the sort of absurdity that this principle of making exemptions according to age leads to. Why should a person who has, let us say, the income that I have been receiving for the last few years, namely, $6,000 a year, receive an extra exemption of $500 a year just because he or she is 65 years of age or over? Surely no argument can be made for that sort of thing, but an argument can be made for the change that was not made, namely, raising the exemptions of all persons in the low-income groups by $500.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are not many of them.
Mr. MaeINNIS: If my hon. friend was not a preacher I would doubt his word. However, since he is, I suppose I have to take his statement, but he will have, when he goes home to Fort William, to square it with the people there.
When the minister made the proposal in his budget speech the other evening he said at page 4067 of Hansard:
Having in mind the large number of elderly people living on small fixed incomes, and out of consideration for the particular trials and increased expenditures that usually come with advancing years, I am proposing that an additional exemption of $500 be granted to a taxpayer of sixty-five years of age or over.
It is too bad that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) did not have a talk with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) before he drafted the amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act last session. It is
too bad that the latter did not have an opportunity to tell the Minister of Finance of the troubles and trials of people in the seventy years of age group, and the increased income they should have because of their increasing disabilities. Evidently that was not done.
I agree with the minister that many in the sixty-five years and over group find it difficult to exist on their present incomes, but I want to tell him that very few of those who need assistance and need it most, will be helped by the exemption, because their incomes are not high enough to be taxed. Surely these are the people who need help.
Having mentioned the old age pensions, let me compare these exemptions with the government's old age pension policy. The old age pension is $30 a month, or $360 a year. Remember also, that if the wife of a pensioner is not eligible in her own right, although she may be sixty-five years of age and cannot earn an income, there is no contribution on her behalf. The two of them have to get along on $360 a year if they have no extra income. If they have extra income, a single person can have income up to $600. A married couple can have an income up to $1,080. If, however, the income goes above these amounts their pension is reduced accordingly.
Surely there must be something wrong with the sort of reasoning that gives an increased exemption to a person who has an income of $750 or over, if single, and $1,500 or any amount over that, if married, and then refuses to allow to a single person the right to increase his income over $600 without being penalized, or a married couple to increase their income over $1,080 without penalty.
Old age pensioners, as I have pointed out, cannot receive benefits. This provision does not allow for it, because under it their incomes are not high enough. According to the 1947 report on the Old Age Pensions Act, forty per cent or more of the population of Canada at. the age of seventy or over are now in receipt of old age pensions. The number last year was, I believe, 209,029. I do not know how many will benefit under the government's proposal for raising the exemption, but I am satisfied that it is not anywhere near one-half this number. I would say the figure would be about 80.000, or about eight per cent of all persons sixty-five years of age and over.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The total number is 275,000.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Does the minister say the total number of old age pensioners is 275,000? My figure was for the year ended March 31, 1947.
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

The economic condition of persons seventy years of age and over is tersely, and I presume correctly, put in the green book containing the government's proposals to the provinces in 1945. At page 37 I find, under the heading of "Deficiencies of the present scheme", that is to say, the scheme we have now, the following:
The means test is generally recognized as undesirable after a certain age. It has been noted that about 40 per cent of all persons of seventy years of age and over make application, satisfy the means test requirements and receive pensions. There is little doubt that a very considerable number in addition are not able entirely to support themselves, but are dependent upon their family, and refrain from applying for pensions because of embarrassment occasioned by the means test.
None of these people will benefit under these exemptions. Then, as regards those in the sixty-five to sixty-nine age group, the same green book states:
The minimum age of seventy, though convenient as a dividing line with respect to the payment of any kind of universal old age pension, is nevertheless too high in a number of eases of actual need. A strong case can be made for reducing the age limit to sixty-five in order to provide assistance, at least for those in the age group sixty-five-sixty-nine, who are actually in need.
It seems to me it would be much better, and it would serve a much greater need, if the government, instead of allowing additional exemptions to those who least need them, had done something to help those who are in dire circumstances.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that income tax on the age basis is wrong in principle, that the people who need assistance are those whose incomes are not sufficient for a standard of living that can maintain health and decency. Therefore, income tax exemptions should apply not only on the income of persons of sixty-five years of age and over but on all incomes below $1,250 for single and $2,500 for married persons.
By way of a little advice to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, I would say that the government's proposals for increased exemptions for persons of sixty-five years of age and over make the means test for old age pensions more illogical than ever, and I suggest that he bring in a bill, even at this session, to eliminate that. There is no longer any logic or justice in maintaining it after the proposals for the new income tax exemptions have been approved. The abolition is also, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) reminds me, mentioned in the proposals set out in the green book, in which the government agreed to assume the whole pension without a means test for persons seventy years of age and over.
[Mr. Maclnnis.)
I am not quite sure, but I believe the minister said in his budget speech that one of the reasons for not raising exemptions in the lower income groups was the fear of its inflationary effect. On page 4056 of Hansard he said:
As consumers, we are bidding eagerly for a limited supply of goods, throwing into the auction- not only most of our current incomes but also part of our past savings and additional funds obtained by instalment credit.
I am wondering whether the minister realized the implication of his own words. Speaking in the budget debate last year, I drew attention to the fact that instalment buying was on the increase and that this could mean one thing only, and that was that people were not able to buy the necessities of life with their current income. If that was the case a year ago, it is more the case this year, because prices have risen considerably in the meantime.
In a recent report by the dominion bureau of statistics, it is stated that, although the money value of retail sales is still increasing, the volume of goods sold has been decreasing since October of last year, and that the decrease in volume since that time is about ten per cent. What is happening, then, is this, that as consumers we are paying more money for fewer goods. To those in the higher income brackets that is not of very great importance. It means one of two things. They can reduce their savings or they can reduce their luxury buying; but, as far as the essentials or the necessities of life are concerned, they can still buy sufficient to maintain their living standards. For those in the lower income groups the situation is quite different, For them higher prices mean a lowering of living standards and also going into debt. That situation needs to be rectified, in my opinion, as soon as possible. One way of rectifying it is by raising the exemptions and giving more income to those in the lower income groups, even if this has to be done by raising taxes in the higher income brackets.
The drastic increase in prices in the last year and a half or two years make the raising of the exemptions in the low-income groups nothing more than a straight matter of justice. Let us just see what the situation is. The exemption of $750 for a single person and of $1,500 for a married couple came into effect on January 1, 1947. The cost of living index at that time was 127. The index today, as it appears in the minister's budget statistics, is 152, or in other words, there is a rise of approximately twenty per cent in the cost of living. This means'that the $750 of January 1, 1947, is worth only $600 now and that the $1,500 is worth only $1,200 now. Yet with all

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
those facts before him, the Minister of Finance and the government expect the people of this country to carry on as if nothing were wrong. I am afraid they will have a rude shock some day, because you cannot treat people over a period of time in that fashion, without producing certain changes in their mental outlook and on their loyalties.
Considerable was said, Mr. Speaker, about the large surplus announced by the Minister of Finance. I will say at once that I have no objection whatever to the Minister of Finance showing a large surplus. Any objections that I have in the matter are based not on the size of the surplus but on the way in which the surplus was raised. Too much of it was raised by indirect taxes and too little from direct taxes, at a time when incomes in certain quarters were at an all-time high. It seems to me that if the government at this time did not provide for a substantial surplus, it would be subject to severe censure by the people of this country. We have a huge debt occasioned by two wars and ten years of depression. Surely we are not to continue paying interest on that debt forever or until, if economic conditions get bad-as they were before the war-we shall be adding again to the debt.
I should like to point out to hon. members who are objecting 'to this budget that the interest on the national debt last year, in 1947, was $466 million, or more than twenty-one per cent of the total expenditures. May I also point out that that is only $50 million less than the total estimated revenue for the year 1938, just ten years ago.
I think it was the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) who the other day said something about being old-fashioned. I may be old-fashioned. I do not like debt and I do not think debt is any better for a country than it is for an individual. The time when we should budget to reduce the debt is a time like the present when the government finds itself in the same position as the people who appeared before the prices committee who say, according to their evidence, that they made money in spite of themselves. They said they could not help it. When it was pointed out that their profits were unduly high, they replied that they just could not help it, that they made the extra money because the market was that way; and the market was that way because the government removed price control. Because the government did not maintain price controls, it has more money than it budgeted
for; and just because it has that, I think the country should get the benefit of it in reduced debt.
There are a number of other items I should like to refer to, but I want to have time to refer briefly to some comments made by the financial critic for the official opposition. I am doing that because the hon. member made a plea for clear thinking. Because he made a plea for clear thinking, I took the trouble to read his speech most carefully, and I am bound to say that seldom have I read a speech that is so full of cliches and catch-phrases as is the speech of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario last Friday. I hope the hon. gentleman will pardon me for saying that, because I have a high regard for him. But as he in the same speech also made a plea for intellectual honesty, I am bound to say what I have said.
I shall refer to only two or three points. At page 4242 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
I am sure everyone will agree, even those who do not share the view that private enterprise is the solution to our economic^ problems, that the lifeblood of private enterprise is that new and small businesses should constantly be coming into the picture and be encouraged to become bigger.
It usually happens that a small industry does get bigger, but as it gets bigger, the smaller ones have a tendency to disappear. I have no objection to the hon. gentleman wanting small industries because they are the lifeblood of the country, but when at the same time he says he hopes they will get bigger I really cannot understand him.

speechtext: You would not want them to get smaller, would you?

speechtext: The average life of an industry in the United States is eight years. From the way they were going under during the ten years between 1930 and 1939, I do not know whether their span of life is longer in this country, but we may find out.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He means he hopes they will prosper.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I hope so, too. Then at page 4247 of Hansard the hon. member gets down to the matter of saving. He said:
I am going to say a word about savings, though one is almost self-conscious in talking about savings these days. Many people think that is a silly old-fashioned thing only talked about by people who are still living in the nineteenth century. My own belief is that there is great danger in the view which is so widely held that wealth consists in pieces of paper. If only we could think of it in terms of goods I believe we would be much more sensible. If we would also remember that at the present
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

time we are living largely on savings, as I say both government realizations and the savings of private 'individuals, who are spending more than they are saving, as a whole, we would appreciate how important it is.
I think we should be clear in our own minds as to what are savings, because I do not think the hon. gentleman is clear. What are savings? My own definition is that savings are that part of the national income not spent on consumption goods, if it is invested in capital goods for the production of new wealth. As long as savings can be invested in producing new wealth, saving is desirable. When savings cannot be used in that way, saving becomes socially undesirable; it becomes hoarding, and is a detriment rather than a benefit to the economy. As a matter of fact, anyone who believes that the money used to exchange the goods we produce is wealth is backward in his economics. It is so elementary that it is hardly necessary to refer to it.
The fact of the matter is that at present we are not living off our capital; that is, we are not consuming capital without replacing it. In one or two places during his speech the minister said that a part of our trouble was that we were trying to replace too much capital too quickly. I am going to quote some figures, not in dollars but in terms of production.

I see, Mr. Speaker, you are rising to tell me that my time is up, and I shall draw my remarks to a conclusion. I say we are living in dangerous times. When people have proven by their stand on various questions over periods of years that they have integrity, that they have understanding and that they believe in democracy, then other people, even if they do not like their philosophy, should not for political purposes try to confuse the minds of the people; because confusion is dangerous.
(Translation):
Mr. GEORGES H. HEON (Argenteuil): Mr. Speaker, the budget proposals for the current fiscal year, presented to this house on May 18, may have seemed perfectly orthodox to those who drafted them, but they were received by our aggravated people with no more enthusiasm than was displayed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in presenting them or by hon. members in digesting them. This statement of the government's tax policy has brought no relief, no easing of the burden of income tax which the taxpayer of less than sixty-five years of age has to bear, whether he be a farmer, a merchant, an industrialist, a professor, an office employee, a professional or a labourer.
Among the chief victims of this new tax policy will be the heads of families, especially in the province of Quebec, where large families are not uncommon. Already they were overburdened by those numerous and irritating taxes, by the dwindling away of their pay envelopes from which were deducted the taxes collected at the source, unemployment insurance contributions and the like, by the ever-increasing cost of food and clothing and by a disheartening decline in the buying power of our Canadian dollar.
In fact, because tax exemptions remain unchanged while the people's purchasing power has been cut down by the higher cost of living, the income tax, though remaining at the same level, may well be considered higher in comparison with former years. This very afternoon, I went to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics to get definite information on the cost of living index.
In April of 1947, it stood at 130-6 while today, May 27, 1948, it has reached 151-6, highest point in the history of this country, not excepting the period that followed the first great war, although at the time there were no such things as controls and cyclical budgeting.
In the past twelve months therefore, the cost of living index has gone up 21 points. In view of this inordinate increase, taxes and exemptions that remain at the same level as last year are causing taxpayers a substantial degree of hardship of which they have good cause to complain. Some waggish newsman has called these proposals a "vinegar budget". Well, many a taxpayer will agree that the expression is sufficiently bitter to describe their feeling in the matter.
Canadian taxpayers, especially those who supported this government in the 1945 general election, had a right to expect a substantial tax cut. In fact, in the Liberal party's 1945 election platform, which I have before me as I speak, I find at pages 4 and 13 the following pledges:
Tax reductions-the Liberal government will gradually reduce taxes when the war is over.
Taxes will be lowered in order to release the people's purchasing power and give Canadians prosperity, employment and freedom.
Then, again at page 7:
Tax reductions-war taxes will be lowered or repealed on May 11, 1945. Consumer goods will soon be back on the market at 1941 prices. Income tax reductions will come next.
The steady rise in the cost of living index which has now climbed to 151-6 and the government's tax policy are a far cry from the
The Budget-Mr. Heon

pledges I have just quoted. If that is what is understood by cyclical budgeting, a system praised so highly by various theorists, it were perhaps better to return to the old principle that allowed the taxpayer to benefit fully from any accumulated surplus. This year, the apparent surplus amounts to $679 million, and will be devoted almost exclusively to reducing the national debt that now reaches the astronomical figure of $12,378 million. Is it expected that we shall pay off this debt, resulting largely from our economic and military assistance to Great Britain, by means of cyclical financing? Shall we stick to this new policy of debt reduction by keeping taxation at present levels until the debt is wiped out? I am afraid the Canadian taxpayer will not have the patience to go that far, because after all, he is the one who pays.
During the war, Canadians sacrificed much in the way of life, money and labour. They now have a right to expect tax relief when a huge surplus is declared. It is fitting that part only, say half of this astounding surplus, be applied to debt reduction. And in all fairness and equity the other half should be used to relieve the taxpayer, particularly in those years of high costs. In recent years, Canada has given or loaned without security billions and millions to nations more powerful than itself. Such munificence made us feel strong, wealthy and able to dispose of staggering amounts. It is therefore very hard to understand how today, we must suddenly clamp down and deprive the taxpayers of reductions fully justified by the high cost of living and the surplus declared.
I repeat that the man in the street, the ordinary civil servant, the salaried man of the so-called1 "white-collar" class, the good industrial worker and above all the family man who, without flinching, witnessed the dance of billions during the war and to whom every promise was given that we might win the war, have a right to complain about those low exemptions and high taxes. Some people go on repeating that Canada has become with the last two great wars a great international power and that she plays a leading part in foreign affairs. Let us be careful lest a too heavy burden of taxes, too long maintained, seem too high a price to pay for the privilege of contributing, from the background, in the making of peace treaties, and lest Canadians decide at last to start minding their own business by

looking after their own social and financial security.
We have heard a lot lately about social justice and just salaries; countless labour disputes have broken out these last twelve months and our conciliation and arbitration boards have had their hands full, settling these disputes. It can be stated in a general way that, as a result of this arbitration workers have obtained redress of their grievances while employers have paid the salaries which their income allowed. However, the cost of living has reached the highest level yet, and might increase still further. There will surely be more such claims from the ranks of labour and as most employers will be in no position to increase wages indefinitely, strikes, some of them possibly violent, will paralyse our economy. It is therefore up to the government to follow the only course that is left open if these new conflicts are to be avoided. Income tax exemptions must therefore be raised substantially, both for single people and married people with dependents.
It is unfortunate that the government did not see fit to take note of the suggestions contained in the brief submitted by the Catholic bishops of Quebec, and by other religious denominations, respectfully suggesting an inorease of income tax exemptions. I sincerely hope those suggestions will eventually be followed. They are distinguished by their authoritative nature and their plain common sense.
Let us have a look at today's exemptions:
For single persons, the exemption is $750. In view of the high cost of board, clothing, and other necessaries, and of room or apartment rent, how can a single man save anything and prepare to establish a home? This paltry exemption is not far from being antisocial and anti-religious and it should, in my opinion, be raised to $1,500.
For married persons, the exemption is now $1,500. In their case also the cost of living fritters down the exemption enough to make it insignificant, greatly reduces opportunities for saving and establishing a comfortable and modern home. The exemption should be raised to $2,400, which would ensure a reasonable margin of financial security and encourage thrift and industry.
But, to my mind at least, it is particularly with regard to children that the present exemption is distinctly antisocial. At the present time, if a child benefits from the family allow-

The Budget-Mr. Dorion
ance which cannot exceed $120 a year, the exemption is $100, which makes up a total of $220.
With the pace and requirements of modern life, who can properly feed, bring up, clothe, give an education to a child on $220 a year? It is impossible and even if parents should resort to cyclical finance and jugglery, they will not be able to make both ends meet without denying themselves or borrowing money.
In the case of children over 15 years of age and not in receipt of family allowances, the present exemption is $300. It is well known that at the age of 15, a child usually has completed his elementary course and is ready to undertake classical studies or enter some other institution of higher learning. He needs an entirely new wardrobe, because he has grown up. Clothing, books, pocket money, and fairly high boarding and tuition fees must be provided for. How can parents meet all these necessary expenditures with $300? As everyone knows, that is quite impossible, so much so that higher studies are often abandoned for lack of money or savings. It therefore seems that both in order to encourage large families and to facilitate higher or specialized studies among our people, a total exemption of $500 for each child would be essential, especially in view of the high cost of living. To my mind, such an investment would bring valuable dividends in the future and ensure the living and educational standard to which the younger generation is fully entitled.
It is all very well to practise internationalism, to accumulate huge surpluses, but it is still better and much more practical to grant our own people religious, social and economic security. Tax exemptions should be immediately increased to $1,500 for single people and $2,400 for married people, with an additional exemption of $500 per child. That would prove an excellent means of disposing of our estimated or anticipated surplus.
Since the present budget offers no relief to the farmer, the wage-earner or salaried man of less than 65 years of age-except for the abolition of the tax on alarm clocks, watches, bets on horse races, vinegar and a few consumer goods-and since my electors are dissatisfied with the government for having failed to reduce the income tax or tax exemptions, I shall have to vote against the motion.
Next year, with general elections in sight its system of cyclical financing or financial cycling will no doubt enable the government to grant substantial income tax reductions. Should these reductions be of the kind I have
been advocating tonight, and which should have been granted in the present budget, I shall support them by my vote.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel called upon to say a few words on this budget.
First, I must say that, like at least 90 per cent of the Canadian taxpayers, I was deeply and painfully shocked to realize that as I shall presently show-this budget is but a further indication of the anti-family and antisocial policies which have victimized us for so long.
Honest and conscientious citizens are all the more disappointed in finding that this anti-family policy, which is becoming more and more apparent in our legislation, is but an offshoot of an economic system managed by an irresponsible bureaucracy which seems bent on destroying or at least weakening the family sole basic unit of a well-organized society.
I know that many hon. members to your right, Mr. Speaker, watch the developments of this policy with fear; I realize that many of them eagerly wish for more human legislation that will be kinder to families. I know what many of them think of this budget but, unfortunately, party discipline compels them to vote for it though they would like to disapprove and censure the government's policy in this instance.
Surely, I need not speak at great length to prove that the existence and expansion of the family are essential to social life.
To confirm my statement I need only quote the late and lamented Cardinal Villeneuve.
During a week to social studies, in 1923, Cardinal Villeneuve, at that time Father Villeneuve, said, in Montreal, in reference to the family considered as social unit:
Thus family, not the individual, is the social unit; it is a simple body in society, made up of elements so numerous and so different. To understand social order, one has to begin with the family. Political society is superimposed upon organized families, without however destroying them.
And further on:
Public legislation, therefore, ladies and gentlemen, should take scrupulous and constant care not to crush or break up the family, a cell in the social structure. On the contrary, according to Antoine, it is the great and peremptory duty of the legislator to recognize, protect, and strengthen the fundamental rights which the family has received, not from the state, but from God, author of nature.
4484
The Budget-Mr. Dorion

Social organization aims today at protecting, apparently at least, through an abundance of texts, the individual, his fortune, his political rights, his outside relations with his neighbours, but it holds nothing or practically nothing, it destroys all, or nearly all of what is left of old legal traditions that could protect the family against so many undermining assaults. It kills rather the principles of life, the organic ties which sustain the family, and through the family it affects society, and through society human happiness. Neither the authority of the father, nor the primacy of the husband, nor the subordination of the son and the servant, nor the vital indissolubility >and the exclusive unity of the matrimonial tie are preserved, rather they are surrendered for the sake of peace, often quite gladly.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that to a certain extent that statement contains a criticism that applies to the budget we are now discussing. Indeed, one of the anti-family aspects of this budget is the fact that, against the hopes of everybody, the wishes of every taxpayer and the request of every family head, no tax reduction has been announced.
There is no doubt that in view of the huge surplus announced by the minister, he should have raised to at least S2,500 the taxable minimum of the married taxpayer. I shall not take time to go over all the reasons already given in support of that request, but there is no doubt that such a change is absolutely necessary because of the increase in the cost of living.
The government should at least have granted relief to heads of families by increasing the exemption to which he is entitled for his children. It is astounding to see how, through this income tax measure, parents are penalized for wishing to give their children the care and education they require. It seems that none of those responsible for the present state of affairs have the slightest notion of what it means to support a son or daughter who wishes to continue his or her studies. There is another objectionable feature in the present Income Tax Act. That is the deduction at the source irrespective of the type of employment. In my constituency, for instance, and in others too, there are quite a number of logging-camps which for part of the year hire only farmers, sailors or fishermen to work in the woods during the off-season.
Were the wages paid these loggers put on a yearly basis, they would be liable to income

tax; so the employers have to deduct it at the source.
Now, at the end of the year, those people have to file returns and produce receipts which are often mislaid, and afterwards they have to wait nearly a year before being refunded what has been deducted from their salary. That system causes much inconvenience and trouble, in addition to considerable administration expenses. What is more serious, those taxpayers are generally in urgent need of that money, which is theirs anyway, and as often as not their families have to suffer.
Why does not the government eliminate all those difficulties by deciding, for instance, that the salary of certain seasonal employees will no longer be subject to such a deduction? Since a distinction is made between seasonal and regular employment in other legislation, for example in the Unemployment Insurance Act, why should it not also be done in the case of the Income Tax Act?
In this connection, there is also another matter which I should like to point out. It so happens that quite a number of young people who, during the war, had left their homes to work in industrial plants have gone back to their rural communities. They have settled there, have married and have resumed an occupation which pays less than their wartime jobs, their income being, at times, barely sufficient to provide a living for their new families.
Now a great number of these new heads of families are at present receiving from the Income Tax Division certain claims for balances owing for 1943, 1944 and 1945. I know of many cases where these young bread-winners have had to deny their families the necessities of life in order to repay the revenue department.
This makes for social unrest. I would therefore ask the government to cancel all claims of less than $500, against heads of families, for income tax levied during the war years. The total of those claims would certainly not be very large and it would mean a great relief for those young families.
Mr. Speaker, the government has been swamped with requests for special consideration to family men. The bishops' request for higher exemptions is significant. They had given it much thought and they were surely not looking after their own interests. I agree

The Budget-Mr. Lacombe
that during the war every Canadian without exception was expected to contribute fully to the war effort. Perhaps it is necessary to impose unduly high taxes during tihe war, but I contend that the government is violating the rights of the family by keeping the taxes at the same level in peacetime.
I was particularly impressed by the fact that the minister did not deem it advisable to grant tax reductions, although he encouraged night clubs, places of entertainment and similar organizations, by abolishing the tax formerly levied upon tihem. It is admittedly a strange attitude. I remember that on the day following the budget speech, newspapers were filled with advertisements from places of amusement, night clubs and so forth, soliciting young people's increasing patronage.
Taxes still fall heavily upon the shoulders of the family man, while habitues of night clubs and other places of amusement are encouraged to patronize such places which certainly do not help bring the family closer together.
As most of those who seek this kind of entertainment are single, everything seems planned to entice them away from their family.
Mr. Speaker, if our legislation were imbued with a more Christian, a sounder moral spirit, there would be no need to fear the menace that is now hanging over society.
It is useless to pass social legislation if we give it the anti-family character found in so many of our enactments such as the Family Allowances Act with its decreasing rate, the various housing acts that promote the building of two and three-roomed apartments and many other pieces of legislation. Such enactments can never be effective; they will give maximum results only if based on the interests of the family rather than on those of the individual.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget produced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) will greatly deceive the taxpayers in the low-income brackets. The burden of taxation is still too heavy for the average wage earner with dependents. A government cannot proclaim a surplus and at the same time leave under the burden of taxation and excessive cost of living those who work and toil in the interests of their families and of society.
Everything can be bought at a ransom price because the administration could not or did not want to foresee the present situation. Family allowances have become null and void because the government allowed trusts to accumulate shameful profits at the expense of our families. In these difficult times the good elements still remaining in democracy should unite against the profiteers who sooner or later will ruin it in favour of communism.
The time has come to hand out to the diplomats and public men, responsible for the communist invasion which is now threatening civilization., the treatment they deserve. Many times I have raised this issue in this chamber. I have pointed out often enough the inherent danger of the government's attitude toward communist Russia and its satellites, and I believe I can free myself from the responsibility for the impending danger which will soon destroy the civilized world.
So far as I am concerned, I cannot support the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) when he asks for appropriations for the carrying out of a blameable policy. For a long time, when he was Minister of Justice, he refused to outlaw the communist party in Canada. Why, then, did the minister show such haste in appointing an ambassador to the government of Yugoslavia, a renowned persecutor of bishops and religion? Why manifest this open sympathy toward the deceiving and communist government of Poland? Why mobilize the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in order to locate property which belongs to the church and which the Polish government wished to misappropriate and steal in communist fashion?
Why tolerate in Canada the hatred and treason of the Labour-Progressive party, while refusing to appoint an ambassador to the Vatican, whose supreme appeal to charity, justice and peace is the only hope in these extremely difficult times?
The nations refused to receive the illustrious pontiff's appeal to charity, justice and peace. Because they ignore the only logical advice, the allied nations won the war twice and lost peace twice within thirty years.
What has happened to the war aims of the united nations? Christianity was sacrificed to the communists by the very people who claimed they were defending it. In the
The Budget-Mr. Lacomhe

underworld of international diplomacy Poland was sacrificed with the shameful co-operation of the Canadian government, this same government which declared war when the German hordes were dominating that country, which was invaded and dismembered many times in history.
What did our rulers do? When Poland was agonizing in devastation and ruin, they officially recognized the usurping and communist government of Lublin. As servants of Soviet Russia, they came to terms with the invertebrate people of Yalta in order to impose upon Poland the communist bandits who are now presiding over the destinies of that country.
This hypocrisy has gone far enough. Nobody will believe that an atheistic government was instituted in Poland without the connivance and co-operation of the present government. Tomorrow we shall see the government imposing compulsory military service in order to stop communist Russia, which only recently our government was cherishing, feeding, equipping and arming on behalf of the great principles of the Atlantic charter, which never even existed. This is national and international life. Insidious propaganda, condemn-able concealments, lies-everything is used in order to deceive the people. The government proceeded gradually when it imposed upon the population its policy of participating in the war, its mobilization and conscription.
Stalin also proceeded gradually in his policy of invasion. The government of Canada and the Secretary of State for External Affairs freely opened the door for him by recognizing the satellite of the Russian dictator as the communist government of Poland. We shall soon be called to the colours. Once more Canada will sacrifice its blood and its economy through the error of the government, which contributed to installing communism in Poland first, and then in the other satellite countries of Russia.
The war which is threatening the world will be more horrible than what we have yet seen. Whole countries will be destroyed by infernal inventions whose power will be irresistible and frightful. Death germs will be scattered everywhere. Those responsible for this calamity will pose as crusaders. Nobody will refuse to defend Canada if this country is attacked. But I know some people upon whom history will cast a slur because unconsciously they gave away our country to communism. These people will still require the obligation to serve. Since it is easier, but less noble, to vote other people's death rather than one's own, once more they will vote the sacrifice of our sons.

Hiding in remoteness, they will be awaiting fearfully a guiding light in the night into which their disastrous policies have plunged the world. Because they could not prepare peace, they are now preparing wTar. In this twentieth century in the Christian era, we are reverting to barbarism through the selfish interests of predatory nations. We are being led to the abyss by military and financial imperialism. The true doctrine of charity and love was trampled upon. The solemn warnings of the Vatican were ignored by Canada as well as by other countries. As an illustration, I only wish to quote the following excerpt from the Vatican organ, L'Osservatore Romano:
Si vis pacem, para helium . . .
Vatican City (PA)-The Osservatore Romano, the official organ of the Vatican, stated today that the world is reverting to the times of the old principle "Si vis pacem, para helium", "if you want peace, get ready for war."
Before the Christian civilization, this was the only valid principle. But Christianity has changed this principle; it proclaims: "If you want peace, prepare for peace."
According to certain Vatican sources, this editorial was written by Count Guiseppe Della Torre. It also contained this sentence: "If we are compelled to replace faith by strength, even in a defensive manner, it is because Christianity is far below its object." Is it not deplorable to witness what is now going on? Let no one eulogize democracy, a corrupt and corrupting regime. As we know it today, it is not worth while fighting for it. When governments instil into it the dose of Christianity which it requires to survive, then and then only will it deserve our protection.
The best way to combat communism is to solve the problem of slums and replace them by dwellings worthy of the average man and his family. In this twentieth century is it decent to tolerate in our midst, all these shacks and slums? The housing problem is a national one. It is up to the federal government to solve it. Let the government take money wherever it can. Economic liberalism has lasted too long. It is the source of the worst infringements. The Canadian people are fed up with this laissez-faire policy of the government. The average families are shamefully exploited by the ruthless trusts. Some high-class robbers are controlling certain companies which dominate our Canadian politics.
One of the most disgusting instances can be found in the profits accumulated on the sales of butter by Canada Packers. During a short term of eleven months, this company made more profits than during the previous twenty years. And this disgraceful robbery goes on under the eyes of a servile government

The Budget-Mr. Lacombe
which reserves all its sympathies for these trusts which are essential to its electoral organization. The exploitation of the people by trusts is the life source of communism.
To this add the co-operation of the government when Poland was betrayed by the most powerful nations on earth, in favour of communist Russia, when they officially recognized the impostor government of Lublin, and then you have the lamentable picture of the leadership of communism in the world.
Czechoslovakia was sacrificed at Munich by five statesmen who were branded by history: Stalin, Hitler, Mussolini, Daladier and Chamberlain. Since then, that country seems to have lost all faith in the great nations which then were at the maximum of their power. It was the same Stalin who stabbed Poland in order better to dominate it. Poland had to undergo the shame of treason; her political leaders are now the victims of the communist gestapo.
Smaller nations were misled by the lies and hypocrisy of powerful democracies and proud dictatorships. Their leaders were not up to their duties, since they were bound by the selfish interests of financial imperialism which has been dominating history and governments for many years. They bear the responsibility for the present situation. Even here in Canada, for many years the motto of the government is the same as Talleyrand's: "Governing means dissimulating." The same situation exists throughout the world. Truth, charity and justice have been replaced by a policy of falsehood, persecution and hatred. The Vatican, where Pope Pius XII is reigning, is the greatest power in the world, because this illustrious pontiff is always preaching a doctrine of charity, peace and love. I have often asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs to appoint an ambassador to the Vatican. The minister does not seem to be interested in the Vatican. He answers by appointing an ambassador to Marshal Tito, the persecutor of the primate of the church of Yugoslavia. This is an insult to five million Roman Catholics in Canada, and an insult to Christianism. The minister and the government do not like me to bring forth this most important matter. They turn a deaf ear to it; but some day they will wake up facing a situation beyond remedy, in Canada and in the rest of the world, for which they will be responsible.
When will political leaders have enough courage to assume their responsibilities and squarely face events? From that day Canada
will not be called upon to sacrifice her sons and her economy every ten or twenty years in disastrous and useless wars.
Finally, may I mention a regrettable event which happened recently. The United States refused to consider as persona grata a certain diplomat recently arrived from Czechoslovakia; and our government readily accepted the same individual as consul of his country in Canada. One would think our country has become the refuge of all communist miscreants intent on promoting revolutions and causing trouble.
If a member of this house introduces a bill to outlaw the communist or the Labour-Progressive party in Canada, immediately an endless debate starts, while it would be preferable to remain silent so that the bill could go through. Eventually we shall be convinced that communism is well protected in this country. Such an attitude is not new. During the 1936 session the Liberal party voted the repeal of section 98 of the criminal code, which prohibited all unlawful associations and all associations whose purpose was to undermine lawfully constituted authority in Canada.
We have no use for all these communist agents. The government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs should be extremely firm and should send back to their own countries these communists with doublebreasted suits, since among this underworld they are the most affluent and the most powerful. Then only will the Canadian people know security under the protection of the free institutions which Canada won through sacrifice and struggle.
Is he a true Canadian who allows and tolerates the formation of communist cells in our country, and then preaches a crusade throughout the world against this obnoxious doctrine? Such a degree of cynicism is beyond me. I have seen so much treachery during the twenty-five years I have been sitting in this house. I have seen so many solemn pledges violated and trampled upon. I have been a witness to such deceitful and insidious propaganda that I do not hesitate to state that one needs courage to witness the political somersaults of certain politicians who are always prepared to sacrifice Canada in the defence of theories which they themselves created and strengthened by helping atheistic and godless Russia at the expense of small but courageous Christian countries which are now agonizing under Stalin's heel. Let these politicians bear this formidable responsibility.
