subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take two hours, if you wish.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -I want to say, Mr. Speaker, first that I would consider myself derelict in my duty if I did not express an opinion on this budget. I am well aware of the fact that some hon. members are anxious to get away. I am also aware of the fact that it is a great disappointment to them. I am equally sure of this fact that their disappointment is no greater than the disappointment the people of Canada had when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) presented his budget. I can assure you, sir, that the people of Canada are getting very little relief today in the way of taxation from the budget which was brought down the other day.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Take forty minutes.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the Minister of Finance spoke the other day he said he was fearful lest the tax concessions which might have been given would be taken by those who were conducting business in this country. In order that I may not be accused of misquoting the Minister of Finance, I shall use his own words. On page 4064 of Hansard the Minister of Finance gave the reason why he did not think tax concessions should be passed on to the general public at this time. He said:
Demands are so excessive in relation to supply that we cannot rely upon competition or other market forces to ensure that the consumer would get the benefit of any general or widespread reductions we might make. Producers or distributors are in a favourable position to gain whatever the treasury gives up, and they could probably find plausible reasons for doing so, notwithstanding the high levels of profits at present.
That is a very weak excuse for the Minister of Finance to give as his reason for not passing
on these tax reductions which all the country expected. It is lamentable that we in this country find ourselves in the position that we dare not reduce the taxes to the common people lest some others in preferred places might take that profit. It speaks very poorly for government policy, if they have no better safeguards for the public than that. Probably the Minister of Finance does not know of any way in which the public can be protected. Perhaps he is not aware that already in this debate proposals have been set forth which would thoroughly protect the people of this country, if these tax concessions had been allowed to be passed on to them.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I wonder whether hon. members on this side of the house have any rights here, and whether they can be allowed to proceed with their speeches without further interruption from the other side of the house. I think it is about time that a little order was kept here.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not fair.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I ask hon. members behind the curtain not to talk so loudly.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Proceed.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In case the minister may have overlooked the fact that others who have already preceded me in this debate have already offered him some excellent suggestions as to how the public might be safeguarded against the imposition which he thought should come about, I should like to refer to the speech of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) the other day when he gave an effective safeguard for protecting the people in this country, once the government decided to pass on tax concessions to them. If we turn to page 4259 of Hansard of May 21 we shall see that the leader of this group had this to say:
Corporate income tax requires considerable adjustment if proper incentives to all-out production are to be provided, and if we are to ensure the passing on to consumers of benefits resulting from sales tax abolition. Therefore I propose exemption from corporate income tax on a basis that would represent 10 per cent return on capital, this figure to be arrived at by a procedure similar to that used by the board of referees, formerly set up and used by the Minister of Finance; this exemption to be conditional upon the corporation furnishing satisfactory evidence that savings in cost resulting from sales tax abolition have been passed on to consumers.
If the government had taken cognizance of such a measure as that I am sure that the people of Canada would have received the tax concessions which they expected would
The Budget-Mr. Johnston

be passed on to them. There are other ways in which purchasing power to the people could be increased without its being interfered with by any group of persons in this country. The ones to which I refer now are those which have been advocated by this party for some time. The first was the national dividend. In the past we have been criticized for advocating a national dividend. It is true that we are not being criticized to the same extent today that we were in days gone by, because the government saw, and quite properly so, that the things which the Social Credit party were advocating were worthwhile. Therefore they did adopt one of them, and one of the most important ones, namely, the national dividend, except that they called it family allowances. In principle I agree with family allowances, and have always agreed with them, but I object to the manner in which the money is raised to pay family allowances. But from the standpoint of principle it is one of the ways in which the people's interests can be protected, if there was a tax reduction. This might be called incentive controls; incentives which would induce people to produce more, because they would know that the consuming public would have the increased purchasing power with which to buy the increased production.
I do not think there is a party in the house; in fact I am positive there is not a party in the house, certainly not on the opposition side, which has put down its proposals in such clear-cut. fashion for all to see as has the Social Credit party. We may be criticized on them; but had these proposals been used, instead of the taxation club, to beat the consumer into humble submission, I am sure that the average citizen of this country would be much more satisfied than he is today.
The minister seemed to take great delight in the fact that he had a surplus this year of $727 million. May I say this is not the result of sound economics, but rather the result of an outdated orthodox financial system, which this government is endeavouring to make work, even though it may cause severe hardship on the people.
One of the ways in which the government raised this surplus was by taxation. It was not a true surplus in any sense of the word. It was a surplus which was acquired by exorbitant taxation. The sales tax is one of the most outstanding examples of that. The sales tax is one of those taxes that bear most heavily on the people who are least able to stand the strain. Then there are the other taxes which are referred to as indirect or nuisance taxes, and they, too, bear upon the common people more than upon the others. At any

rate, they bear equally upon the rich and the poor, but the rich have the money and the poor have not.
If those taxes had not been so high in the past year; if the government had not used that taxation club to extort this money from the people, the minister's surplus would not have been that grand total of $727 million. Again, the government not only increased their taxes in this budget, but they increased them by twenty-five per cent a while ago in the twenty-five per cent excise tax. The minister might think that is not a tax, but I was interested the other day when I came across the following newspaper article which I clipped out. I think it expresses the thought as well as I could. It is taken from the Ottawa Citizen:
For Mr. Abbott's information.
At least he is getting some worthwhile information today.
Mr. Abbott insists, goodness knows why, that taxes in Canada are lower than in the United States. We would suggest to Mr. Abbott that he try out buying a family car. On the modest purchase of a Ford or a Plymouth he would pay between $500 and $600 more than he would have to pay if he were buying the same type of car in the United States. And if Mr. Abbott thought he would like or could afford something better, say a Chrysler or a Buick, he would pay between $800 and $900 more than if he were buying in the United States. Most of the difference would be represented by taxes-higher Canadian taxes. We hope Mr. Abbott would agree that $500 or $900 would pay (for the average man) a lot of income tax. Also that it would buy a lot of eggs and butter.
So when we thoroughly scrutinize the tax bill which the minister has inflicted upon the people of the country, we find that not only are there all the taxes shown in the budget which he brought down, but there are many other taxes which bear most heavily upon the common, poor people of the country. One outstanding example is that which I have just read from this newspaper.
A car nowadays is not a luxury. It has become a necessity, and when people have to buy these necessities they have to pay an added tax of $500 or $900. Not only is the excise tax inflicted on people through the purchase of automobiles, but it is imposed on other necessities such as electrical equipment for household use, and we find that the veteran today cannot furnish the house he lives in because of excessive taxes which are piled up on top of the already high cost of production. In most cases these are hidden taxes and the manufacturer gets the blame. Of course he is the one who is criticized rather than the one who should be criticized, namely the government.

The Budget-Mr. Johnston
When looking through the budget speech, I was particularly interested in what the minister said about the great surplus. I was interested in the different ways he had of using that surplus. First of all, he thought the surplus would offset a depression. He was going to put that away for a rainy day.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, we are all conversant with the old saying that you cannot tax yourself into prosperity or borrow yourself out of debt; neither can we tax the country into prosperity. That is a certainty. I am not convinced that the minister will be able to fix his financial position by this surplus to such an extent that we shall be relieved of further excessive taxation. So the people must not expect, even though we have had a large surplus this year, that tlhey will not continue to bear heavy taxation in the years to come.
Another way in which the minister was going to use the surplus was to prevent inflation. I could not help wondering, if the minister were really sincere that this surplus would help to offset inflation, and, if there is a severe danger of inflation in this country, why he should not have postponed the payment of the compulsory savings. By paying out the compulsory savings at this time he was putting that amount of money into circulation. If there was already too much money in existence, that may have caused further inflation, but if it did cause inflation he should not have done it but should have postponed it for a year or two.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do you advocate that?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; I would under these circumstances, because what has happened is this. He has given the compulsory savings out today and he is taking them back by increased taxation tomorrow. I say definitely that if there were a danger of inflation the proper thing would have been not to pay out the compulsory savings. He may have had them postponed for a year or so, but he would not have had them confiscated as he has in the excessive taxation program.
He will use the surplus in another way also. I do not know whether he will get all the money he wants out of the $727 million, but he also wants that surplus to pay for the excess of exports over imports. How he will stretch it to that extent I do not know, and if that is not enough he wishes to use it for national defence.
Well, Mr. Speaker, all the good that $727 million would do if another war broke out would not be very much, and I wonder what would happen if another war did break out. Would we limit defence preparations to $727
million? I do not believe he could build more than one battleship with that amount. I am sure that if war broke out we would find more money for defence than that $727 million.
We recall vividly that just before the last war, when this country was in one of the greatest depressions the world had ever seen, when a million and a half people were unemployed, we did not have enough money to keep families from starving to death; yet, almost the day after war was declared, we found millions and billions, in fact so much money that our national debt went from three and a half billion to around seventeen billion gross debt or about fourteen billion net debt.
Where did the money come from? It certainly did not come out of taxes, because the people did not have the money to pay the taxes; and if we can finance war to the extent we did the last time, it seems extremely strange that we cannot finance peace as well.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the present system.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, absolutely it is the present system. The government is endeavouring to make the old worn-out orthodox financial system function in time of prosperity and the only time it will function is in time of scarcity. And the government through its present policy is forcing the country into that position of scarcity.
If the minister is not satisfied with using the $727 million that way, he has another way and that is to reduce the national debt. I never saw' so many uses for a fixed amount of money. On page 4066 of Hansard the minister said, with regard to the national debt:
The general policy for this year should 'be to use our surplus to reduce our debt and thereby to fight inflation in the manner most suited to our type of government and our way of life.
I wonder if the $727 million which the minister has as a surplus would in any way materially reduce our debt? Our net debt is around $13 billion. The interest on that debt alone is in the neighbourhood of $480 million a year. If we reduced that by the approximate $700 million surplus, we would still have a debt of about $12,300 million. I think this will have little meaning as a great achievement by a nearly bankrupt nation. The mere fact that our debt will be reduced to $12,300 million will not in itself make any great difference as far as our financial standing is concerned. For the minister to suggest that this would in any way benefit the nation to any material degree is just pure nonsense. When one considers that we in this country have a national production of around about $13 billion, and that
The Budget-Mr. Johnston

would represent an increase of about twelve per cent or thirteen per cenfi, that should mean that the purchasing power of the people would have to be increased over what it was last year; that is, if they are to be able to buy the total production.
Some might say that part of that will be used for export. True, it will be. But when you export goods, you must bring back goods in return; either that, or you are giving them away. When those goods are brought back here and put upon our market, our people must be in a position financially to buy those goods and consume them. Otherwise we shall have a continuing spiral of unemployment; and we have quite a serious unemployment situation today. Whenever there is a shortage of effective demand for goods and services which the people are producing, then of course you immediately start into a period of unemployment.
I wonder if the minister was sincere about reducing the debt. I hate to accuse him of insincerity, but I must say that I do not think he was sincere. I say that for this reason. I wish to direct your attention for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to a statement which was made by the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Graham Towers, before the banking and commerce committee in 1939. It is found at page 80 of the proceedings of that committee and is in answer to a question by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). The hon. member for Acadia asked this question:
Is it possible for you to imagine any way by which we are ever going to pay the debt we have got?
Mr. Towers replied:
As the debts of the government are an asset of the Canadian people, I do not see much point in the thing; except that, to the extent that the government thinks that the distribution of those assets of the Canadian people-which are its debt-is unsatisfactory, it may take steps to remed.y that distribution in any way that lies within the legislative power; in fact, in anyway, I suppose-by income tax or succession duties or any other action it cares to take.
I should like to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that the governor of the Bank of Canada says this is an asset, and as long as it is owned by the Canadian people it will be all right. But of course we know it is not owned by the Canadian people. I think the estimate at one time was that less than one per cent of the people of Canada owned over * sixty per cent, of the national debt. That is quite a tribute when the rest of Canada must pay homage in the form of interest to these

few. Then Mr. Towers went on further to say, at page 235:
So that all I can say would be this, that in a country where the sum total of public and private debt was decreasing you have a country which is going backward and which is becoming more poverty-stricken. Generally speaking, in a country where you find there is no public and private debt you have a country resembling darkest Africa; there is nothing else.
Following out the opinion of the governor of the Bank of Canada in this regard, if the minister followed the plan which he says he intends to follow, that of reducing the national debt, lie would be putting this country back on the level of darkest Africa; and I do not think anybody will agree with that. I do not agree with it. I do not think that, if we did away with the public debt, it would put this country back on a par with darkest Africa.
But the government has no plan of reducing the national debt. Let there be no mistake about that. If there were a plan, this government would be coming forth with it quickly. If the government were sincere in its endeavour to reduce the national debt, it would do something similar to what the province of Alberta did. Alberta put into operation a plan whereby they would abolish the provincial debt in a matter of twenty-five to thirty years, and it is done on a scientific and logical basis. The dominion government could do that if it wanted to reduce the national debt. I am quite sure that the Minister of Finance agrees with Mr. Towers. If the Minister of Finance wants to find out how to reduce the national debt without putting further burdensome taxation on the people, I would again advise him to refer to the speech made by the hon. member for Peace River, for he clearly outlined the method there.
Some may ask if we should reduce taxation. My personal opinion is that we should reduce it greatly; for certainly the government does not need the taxation which it is putting on the people today. That is evidenced by the fact that the minister had a $727 million surplus. Some of the best monetary authorities in this country agree that we should not at this time go into heavy taxation. Let me refer again to the same governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Towers, when he had this to say about taxation. This was in an argument, or I should say it was in a broadcast put on between different persons; and among those who participated were Mr. Quelch and Mr. Towers. That was on April 4, 1943. Mr. Quelch asked this question of Mr. Towers:
After the war the need will be to encourage private spending. Heavy taxes and public bor-

The Budget-Mr. Johnston
rowing will be contrary to the public welfare. Will the government finance all desirable public projects by credit expansion when necessary?
Mr. Towers replied:
In circumstances such as Mr. Quelch describes,
I would say there would be grounds for government not meeting the entire cost of its programs by taking and drawing on public savings. The desire would be to encourage private spending and make government investment more of a residual item. If part of the necessary money had to come from credit expansion-and the projects were sound and in the public interest-then I should say go ahead.
That is just the opposite, Mr. Speaker, of what the government is doing. It is endeavouring to take from the people at this time all the taxes that the traffic will bear.
It seems to me also, Mr. Speaker, that if the government were really sincere about helping the people of this country, something could have been done to lift the present tax burden, in view of the fact that the government has lifted the tax on pari-mutuels, which is gambling, and on amusements, taxes imposed upon a minority who are best able to pay. Yet the government has not seen fit to do so.
I want to refer to one other thing that seems important to me. During the last few days here we have heard quite a good deal of discussion in regard to communism, which we are trying to combat. We are assisting the people of Europe by giving them goods and services under the European relief plan, and also by giving grants and lend-lease, in order to combat the forces of communism. Yet here at home we are actually fostering the growth of communism by depressing the standards of living of our own people through excessive taxation. I do not know where this logic is leading us. One of the greatest things we could do to combat communism in this country would be to lay off this tremendous, unjustifiable taxation	and raise	the	standard	of
living of our people to such a point that communism would not thrive. That is the proper way to kill communism; make conditions in our country such that people will not tolerate a policy of that kind.
Then for a	moment I	want	to refer	toannuities, because in my view this is another way in which the government has taken a crack at those in the low-income brackets. To make it short,	I should	like	to read	an
editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen the other day dealing with this subject. It said: Annuitants are not rich
There is little basis for the suggestion made from time to time on behalf of insurance companies that "in all too many eases" it is only the well to do who have taken maximum advantage of the lower rates for government annuities. When government annuities were established in 1908	they were	devised to enable
people of moderate means to make provision for a small income in their declining years. That purpose has largely been fulfilled.
In his royal commission inquiry into taxation of annuities four years ago, Mr. Justice Ives, former chief justice of Alberta, found that about 87 per cent of the recipients held contracts for less than $900 a year and that three-quarters of all annuitants were receiving less than $600 a year. In the main those who took out annuities were unable to afford even the maximum of $1,200 a year which the plan permits.
For ten years it was possible to purchase annuities which would return as much as $5,000 a year. Yet at the time of the Ives report there were only 131 annuitants drawing more than $1,200 a year-less than one-half of one per cent of the total.
In 1931 the maximum was reduced to $1,200 a year and it now stands at that figure. At current living costs this is a small amount, especially if it has to cover all the living expenses of the annuitant. Its purchasing power amounts to less than $800 by prewar standards. The government last month sharply increased the premium rates with the result that applications have fallen off. If prices are to remain at anything like their present level the maximum annuity should be raised at least to $1,600'. Otherwise it will be impossible to make provision for a moderate living standard in old age.
Here I say the government has taken away the only opportunity of these people in the low-income brackets to assure themselves of some decent standard of living in their old age.
I am not going to detain the house longer, Mr. Speaker, but I do say the case for reduced taxation is overwhelming, and that at the next election the people will demand the results they wish.
